arXiv:2609.11509v1 [cs.AI] 10 Sep 2026

Extending SMT Solving with Non-Ground Clause Learning

Yasmine Briefs Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarbrücken, Germany Email: {ybriefs,weidenbach}@mpi-inf.mpg.de Affiliation: Graduate School of Computer Science,
Saarland Informatics Campus, Saarbrücken, Germany    Christoph Weidenbach Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarbrücken, Germany Email: {ybriefs,weidenbach}@mpi-inf.mpg.de
Abstract

Quantifier instantiation is currently the main approach to non-ground SMT solving: solvers generate ground instances and solve the resulting ground SMT problems with CDCL(T)-style reasoning. When a conflict is found, conflict analysis learns only a ground clause, even though the conflict comes from instances of non-ground clauses. Yet non-ground reasoning can give exponentially shorter proofs than purely ground reasoning. We propose a calculus that consists of ground instantiations, CDCL(T)-style rules, and non-ground conflict analysis. The solver reasons on ground instances, but the resolution steps of conflict analysis are performed on their original non-ground clauses. This produces learned clauses that are typically more general than the ground conflict. With a suitable strategy, the learned clauses are even non-redundant. We also show how chronological backtracking can be included in SMT solving. Our calculus gives a common setting for CDCL(T)-style SMT solving, a range of instantiation-based procedures, and non-ground clause learning, and we prove that it simulates CDCL, SCL(FOL), SCL(T), and even Resolution.

1 Introduction

Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) has become a central tool in automated reasoning, both in its ground form and in the presence of quantifiers. At the ground level, much of this success is due to CDCL(T) [30, 4], which combines conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) [26] with dedicated theory reasoning. To handle non-ground problems, this architecture is commonly extended by quantifier instantiation [15, 19, 20, 35, 6]: quantified formulas are instantiated, and the resulting ground problems are solved by CDCL(T). Treating solver components, such as CDCL(T), as black boxes is a powerful design principle in automated reasoning. At the same time, many advances in solver efficiency come from integrating these components more tightly with the surrounding search procedure. This observation also motivates a closer integration of quantifier instantiation with CDCL(T). In current SMT solving, quantified clauses are instantiated and the resulting ground conflicts are analyzed by CDCL(T), yielding learned ground clauses. Our goal is to lift this learning step to the non-ground clauses from which the conflicting instances originate. The motivation is not only conceptual: non-ground learning can yield exponentially shorter refutations than purely ground learning [32].

To formalize this idea, we introduce the calculus ICLF (Instantiation-based Clause Learning Framework). The input to ICLF is a first-order clause set modulo theories. A state consists of three main components: a set NN of possibly non-ground clauses, initially containing the input clauses; a set GG of ground instances of clauses in NN, initially empty; and a ground partial model Γ\Gamma, called the trail, also initially empty. The rules of ICLF fall into four groups. Instantiation rules create and delete ground instances of clauses in NN. Ground rules build a partial model for GG in the style of CDCL, by decisions and propagations. Theory rules, such as 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, connect this ground search to a theory solver. Here ICLF abstracts from the concrete theory, or combination of theories, and from the complications involved in theory combination [29, 39, 33, 22]. Finally, conflict analysis rules derive learned clauses. The key point is that, although the clauses in GG are ground, they remain linked to their non-ground origins in NN. During conflict analysis, resolution is therefore performed on these original clauses, not only on their ground instances.

For example, assume that the trail contains, among others, the literals h⁡(a)=g⁡(a)h(a)=g(a), h⁡(a)=ah(a)=a, and g⁡(a)≠ag(a)\neq a. These literals are inconsistent in the theory of equality, since they contradict transitivity. In ICLF, this can be detected by applying 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict with the closure x2≠x3∨x2≠x4∨x3=x4⋅{x2↦h(a),x3↦g(a),x4↦a}x_{2}\neq x_{3}\lor x_{2}\neq x_{4}\lor x_{3}=x_{4}\cdot\{x_{2}\mapsto h(a),x_{3}\mapsto g(a),x_{4}\mapsto a\}, a theory lemma expressing transitivity of equality. We write C⋅σC\cdot\sigma for a clause CC together with a grounding substitution σ\sigma. The instantiated clause C​σC\sigma is used for the ground search, while the associated non-ground clause CC is retained for conflict analysis and resolution. Now assume that h⁡(a)=g⁡(a)h(a)=g(a) was propagated from the closure c≠d∨h(x1)=g(x1)⋅{x1↦a}c\neq d\lor h(x_{1})=g(x_{1})\cdot\{x_{1}\mapsto a\}. An ICLF resolution step unifies the contradictory literals h⁡(x1)=g⁡(x1)h(x_{1})=g(x_{1}) and x2≠x3x_{2}\neq x_{3}, for instance using the most general unifier {x2↦h(x1),x3↦g(x1)}\{x_{2}\mapsto h(x_{1}),x_{3}\mapsto g(x_{1})\}, and derives the clause c≠d∨h⁡(x1)≠x4∨g⁡(x1)=x4c\neq d\lor h(x_{1})\neq x_{4}\lor g(x_{1})=x_{4}. Thus, conflict analysis derives a non-ground clause from a ground conflict.

For first-order clause learning, redundancy is a central issue: a learned clause should ideally not be implied by smaller clauses that are already available. In superposition-based theorem proving [1, 31], redundancy elimination is essential for controlling the search space, but tests such as forward subsumption can be expensive. Simple Clause Learning (SCL) [16, 13], a recent approach that lifts ideas from CDCL to first-order logic by guiding non-ground resolution with a ground partial model, avoids this problem in a different way: its learned clauses are non-redundant by construction. This makes SCL an important starting point for our work. At the same time, SCL is designed around direct reasoning with non-ground clauses; all non-ground clauses have to be considered for propagations and conflicts and conflict analysis leaves little freedom. The goal of ICLF is to keep the useful non-redundancy guarantees of SCL while allowing the ground search to remain close to CDCL(T). Our basic strategy [Definition 2] restricts the rules only enough to ensure that learned clauses are non-redundant with respect to the current set GG of ground instances [Theorem 11]. Thus, implementations can focus propagation and conflict search on GG and use efficient techniques for ground reasoning, without constantly inspecting the full non-ground clause set NN. We also define a stronger, first-order aware strategy [Definition 17], which additionally takes NN into account and guarantees non-redundancy with respect to NN [Theorem 18]. This strategy is closer in spirit to SCL, but still leaves more freedom in conflict analysis. Finally, ICLF contains multiple backtracking rules. They capture CDCL/CDCL(T)-style backtracking, first-order backtracking in the spirit of SCL, and a way to incorporate chronological backtracking [28, 27] into SMT solving.

This flexibility makes ICLF a common setting for several forms of model-based reasoning. In the propositional case, it simulates CDCL. For first-order logic, it simulates SCL and Resolution. Moreover, it simulates clause learning in SCL(T) [11], an adaptation of SCL to the fragment of first-order logic modulo theories without uninterpreted functions and constants. It also captures CDCL(T)-style reasoning on ground clauses modulo theories. Finally, ICLF can be seen as a formal setting for studying a range of instantiation-based SMT procedures: although quantifier instantiation is a standard practical approach, it is usually presented through concrete algorithms and solver architectures rather than as one fixed calculus. In this sense, ICLF is intended as a foundational framework: it identifies which rule restrictions are needed for soundness, non-redundant learning, and termination under suitable restrictions, and which choices can instead be left to strategies and implementations.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 3, we present the calculus ICLF and establish, among other properties, soundness [Theorem 6], termination under suitable restrictions [Theorem 14], and completeness under suitable restrictions [Corollary 16]. In Section 4, we show that ICLF simulates the other calculi mentioned above. This is an extended version of a paper accepted at LPAR 2026 [9]. It contains further examples, lemmas, and explanations in the appendix, as well as all proofs that were omitted from the LPAR paper.

2 Preliminaries

We consider the following standard notions of many-sorted first-order logic without equality [11]. Let Σ=(𝒮,Ω,Π)\Sigma=(\mathcal{S},\Omega,\Pi) be a many-sorted signature where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a finite, non-empty set of sort symbols, Ω\Omega is a non-empty set of function symbols over 𝒮\mathcal{S} and Π\Pi is a finite, non-empty set of predicate symbols over 𝒮\mathcal{S}. We assume that Ω\Omega contains at least one constant of each sort. We additionally assume a set of variables 𝒳\mathcal{X} that contains infinitely many variables of each sort. First-order terms, atoms, literals and substitutions are defined in the usual way. We assume that substitutions are well-sorted and that they have finite domain dom⁡(σ)={x∣x​σ≠x}\dom(\sigma)=\{x\mid x\sigma\neq x\}. We further define the codomain of a substitution as codom⁡(σ)={x​σ∣x∈dom⁡(σ)}\codom(\sigma)=\{x\sigma\mid x\in\dom(\sigma)\}. A clause is a set of literals, which means that duplicate literals are implicitly deleted. If we write a clause as L1∨⋯∨LnL_{1}\lor\dots\lor L_{n}, where the LiL_{i} are literals, we mean {L1}∪⋯∪{Ln}\{L_{1}\}\cup\dots\cup\{L_{n}\}. Likewise, C∨LC\lor L, where CC is a clause and LL is a literal, denotes C∪{L}C\cup\{L\}, and C∨DC\lor D, where CC and DD are clauses, denotes C∪DC\cup D. ⊥\bot denotes the empty clause. We say that a term is ground if it does not contain any variables. We extend this definition to sets of terms, atoms, literals, clauses and clause sets in the obvious way. A substitution σ\sigma is called grounding for a term tt if t​σt\sigma is a ground term. We also extend this definition to atoms, literals and clauses in the obvious way. By comp⁡(L)\comp(L), we denote the complement of a literal LL. We further define a function atom\atom that maps literals to their corresponding atoms. We extend this function to map clauses to the set of atoms of the literals occurring in the clause and clause sets to the set of atoms of the clauses in the clause set. A closure is a pair C⋅σC\cdot\sigma where CC is a clause or ⊤\top and σ\sigma is a grounding substitution for CC. We assume that variables that do not occur in CC are implicitly dropped from σ\sigma, i.e., that dom⁡(σ)\dom(\sigma) only contains variables that occur in CC. Moreover, we assume that codom⁡(σ)\codom(\sigma) is ground. If C∈{⊤,⊥}C\in\{\top,\bot\}, we may write ⊤\top to refer to the closure ⊤⋅{}\top\cdot\{\} and ⊥\bot to refer to the closure ⊥⋅{}\bot\cdot\{\}. Given a clause CC, a closure C⋅σC\cdot\sigma is called an instance of CC. For a clause CC, gnd⁡(C)\gnd(C) denotes the set gnd⁡(C)={C​σ∣σ​ is grounding for C}\gnd(C)=\{C\sigma\mid\sigma\text{ is grounding for $C$}\}. For a clause set NN, gnd⁡(N)=⋃C∈Ngnd⁡(C)\gnd(N)=\bigcup_{C\in N}\gnd(C). The function mgu\mgu denotes the most general unifier of two terms, atoms or literals. We assume that the mgu\mgu does not introduce any fresh variables and is idempotent. Given a ground literal LL and a closure C⋅σC\cdot\sigma, let C=C′∨L1∨⋯∨LnC=C^{\prime}\lor L_{1}\lor\dots\lor L_{n} such that Li​σ=LL_{i}\sigma=L for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\} and LL does not occur in C′​σC^{\prime}\sigma. Further, let μ=mgu⁡(L1,…,Ln)\mu=\mgu(L_{1},\dots,L_{n}). Then, the result of exhaustively factorizing LL in C⋅σC\cdot\sigma is (C′∨L1)​μ⋅σ(C^{\prime}\lor L_{1})\mu\cdot\sigma.

The semantics of many-sorted first-order logic without equality are given by the notion of an algebra. A Σ\Sigma-algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a mapping that assigns (i) a non-empty carrier set S𝒜S^{\mathcal{A}} to every sort S∈𝒮S\in\mathcal{S}, so that S1𝒜∩S2𝒜=∅S_{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\cap S_{2}^{\mathcal{A}}=\emptyset for any distinct sorts S1,S2∈𝒮S_{1},S_{2}\in\mathcal{S}, (ii) a total function f𝒜:S1𝒜×⋯×Sn𝒜→S𝒜f^{\mathcal{A}}:S_{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\times\dots\times S_{n}^{\mathcal{A}}\to S^{\mathcal{A}} to every function symbol f:S1×⋯×Sn→S∈Ωf:S_{1}\times\dots\times S_{n}\to S\in\Omega, (iii) a relation P𝒜⊆S1𝒜×⋯×Sn𝒜P^{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq S_{1}^{\mathcal{A}}\times\dots\times S_{n}^{\mathcal{A}} to every predicate symbol P∈ΠP\in\Pi of arity nn. We assume 𝒯\mathcal{T} to be a theory, i.e., a non-empty set of Σ\Sigma-algebras. 𝒯\mathcal{T} can also be the combination of multiple theories. For instance, as we consider first-order logic without equality, if needed, equality reasoning has to be part of the theory. The semantic entailment relation ⊧\models is defined in the usual way. We write ⊧𝒯\models_{\mathcal{T}} to denote the semantic entailment relation that considers only the Σ\Sigma-algebras 𝒜∈𝒯\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{T}.

A trail is a sequence of annotated, ground literals. Given a trail Γ\Gamma, a ground literal LL is called propositionally true/false in Γ\Gamma if LL/comp⁡(L)\comp(L) occurs in Γ\Gamma. Otherwise, LL is called propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma. The trail in ICLF is always consistent, i.e., no ground literal is propositionally true and propositionally false at the same time. A ground clause CC is called propositionally true in Γ\Gamma if there is a literal L∈CL\in C that is propositionally true in Γ\Gamma. It is called propositionally false in Γ\Gamma if all literals L∈CL\in C are propositionally false in Γ\Gamma. Otherwise, it is called propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma. Trails are interpreted as the conjunction of their literals, clauses are interpreted as the disjunction of their literals and clause sets are interpreted as the conjunction of their clauses. A clause set NN is called satisfiable if there exists a Σ\Sigma-algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that 𝒜⊧N\mathcal{A}\models N. It is called 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable if there exists a Σ\Sigma-algebra 𝒜∈𝒯\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{T} such that 𝒜⊧N\mathcal{A}\models N. Similarly, the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiability of a trail Γ\Gamma is defined. Given a ground set of clauses NN, a trail Γ\Gamma is called a model of NN if all clauses in NN are propositionally true in Γ\Gamma. Two clause sets N1N_{1} and N2N_{2} are called equi-satisfiable if N1N_{1} is satisfiable if and only if N2N_{2} is satisfiable. They are called equi-satisfiable in 𝒯\mathcal{T} if N1N_{1} is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable if and only if N2N_{2} is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable.

Definition 1 (Clause Redundancy).

Let ≺\prec be a well-founded, total, strict ordering on ground literals. We lift this ordering to clauses by its multiset extension. We further define ⪯\preceq to be the reflexive closure of ≺\prec and N⪯C={D∈N∣D⪯C}N^{\preceq C}=\{D\in N\mid D\preceq C\} for a ground clause CC and a ground clause set NN.

A ground clause CC is called redundant with respect to a ground clause set NN and ≺\prec if N⪯C⊧CN^{\preceq C}\models C. A clause CC is called redundant with respect to a clause set NN and ≺\prec if for all C′∈gnd⁡(C)C^{\prime}\in\gnd(C), it holds that C′C^{\prime} is redundant with respect to gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N).

3 The Calculus

We define ICLF as an abstract rewrite system. Its inference rules operate on a state that is a six-tuple (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) where Θ\Theta is a set of ground atoms, Γ\Gamma is the trail, NN is a clause set, GG is a set of closures, kk is a natural number called the decision level, and D⋅τD\cdot\tau is the conflict closure. We define clauses⁡(G)={C​σ∣C⋅σ∈G}\clauses(G)=\{C\sigma\mid C\cdot\sigma\in G\}. The purpose of Θ\Theta is to restrict the set of ground atoms that are currently available in the search for a model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G). Θ\Theta always contains at least all atoms that occur on the trail or in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) [Lemma 5]. The literals in Γ\Gamma are either annotated with a natural number, in which case they are called decisions, or with a closure, in which case they are called propagations, or with 𝒯\mathcal{T}, in which case they are called theory propagations. The decisions in Γ\Gamma are annotated with 1,…,k1,\dots,k in this order [Lemma 5]. The decision level of a decision is its annotation, and the decision level of any other literal in Γ\Gamma is the annotation of the decision closest to its left. If there is no such decision, the decision level of the literal is 00. The decision level of Γ\Gamma is the maximal decision level of a literal in it, or 00 if Γ=ε\Gamma=\varepsilon. For a simpler presentation, NN contains both the initial and the learned clauses and GG contains both the instantiated and the learned closures. If D⋅τ=⊤D\cdot\tau=\top, the algorithm is in the instantiation and model building phase. If D⋅τ=⊥D\cdot\tau=\bot, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-unsatisfiability has been derived. Otherwise, the algorithm is in the conflict analysis phase. The start state for a set of clauses N′N^{\prime} is (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top). We assume that the initial set of clauses N′N^{\prime} does not contain the empty clause. Moreover, we require that the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiability of conjunctions of ground literals is decidable. Instead of using an abstraction function, we write the ground theory literals on the trail directly. An implementation can still use an abstraction function for the ground reasoning.

We first present the four instantiation rules that are used to manage the instances.

Instantiate

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ∪atom(Cσ);Γ;N;G∪{C⋅σ};k;⊤)(\Theta\cup\atom(C\sigma);\Gamma;N;G\cup\{C\cdot\sigma\};k;\top)

given that C∈NC\in N, σ\sigma is grounding for CC, C​σ∉clauses⁡(G)C\sigma\notin\clauses(G) and either C​σC\sigma is not propositionally false in Γ\Gamma or Γ=Γ1​K\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K with K∈{LD⋅τ,L𝒯}K\in\{L^{D\cdot\tau},L^{\mathcal{T}}\} and C​σC\sigma is not propositionally false for Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

Typically, a run starts by applying Instantiate with the empty substitution to all clauses in NN that are already ground. To avoid learning redundant clauses, it is crucial that no instance in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) is false for a proper trail prefix or becomes false by a decision [Definition 2]. The condition on C​σC\sigma being propositionally false ensures that newly added instances preserve this property. Allowing propositionally false instances to be instantiated at all is necessary for following a first-order aware strategy [Definition 17]. To add an arbitrary propositionally false instance, Restart can first be used to return to a trail prefix at which Instantiate is applicable.

ClauseDel

   (Θ;Γ;N⊎{C};G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N\uplus\{C\};G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top)

given that N⊎{C}N\uplus\{C\} and NN are equi-satisfiable in 𝒯\mathcal{T} and there is no grounding σ\sigma with C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G.

Even though it is undecidable in general whether the rule ClauseDel is applicable, there are some sufficient conditions for its applicability, e.g., that CC is subsumed by another clause in NN.

InstanceDel

   (Θ;Γ;N;G⊎{C⋅σ};k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G\uplus\{C\cdot\sigma\};k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top)

given that there is no LC⋅σL^{C\cdot\sigma} in Γ\Gamma.

Although it can make sense to only apply InstanceDel if G⊎{C⋅σ}G\uplus\{C\cdot\sigma\} and GG are equi-satisfiable in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we would like to allow restarts with fresh instances.

AtomDel

   (Θ⊎{A};Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta\uplus\{A\};\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top)

given that A∉atom⁡(Γ)∪atom⁡(clauses⁡(G))A\notin\atom(\Gamma)\cup\atom(\clauses(G)).

The following four rules form the ground rules.

Decide

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;ΓLk+1;N;G;k+1;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma L^{k+1};N;G;k+1;\top)

given that atom⁡(L)∈Θ\atom(L)\in\Theta and LL is propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma.

Propagate

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;ΓLC⋅σ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma L^{C\cdot\sigma};N;G;k;\top)

given that C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G, C​σ=C′∨LC\sigma=C^{\prime}\lor L, C′C^{\prime} is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma and LL is propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma.

Conflict

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

given that D⋅τ∈GD\cdot\tau\in G and D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma.

Restart

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ1;N;G;j;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1};N;G;j;\top)

given that Γ=Γ1​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2} and jj is the decision level of Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

Applying the rule Restart with Γ1=ε\Gamma_{1}=\varepsilon corresponds to a restart in CDCL(T), i.e., a restart on the ground level. We allow restarting with arbitrary trail prefixes, enabling the subsequent application of Instantiate with clauses that would have been propositionally false in Γ\Gamma.

Next, we present the five theory rules.

𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;ΓL𝒯;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma L^{\mathcal{T}};N;G;k;\top)

given that atom⁡(L)∈Θ\atom(L)\in\Theta, Γ⊧𝒯L\Gamma\models_{\mathcal{T}}L and LL is propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma.

Theory propagations are annotated with 𝒯\mathcal{T} and can be explained later when they become relevant during conflict analysis. The condition Γ⊧𝒯L\Gamma\models_{\mathcal{T}}L makes sure that there exists a tautology in the theory from which LL can be propagated.

𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ;N∪{C};G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N\cup\{C\};G;k;\top)

given that C∉NC\notin N and ⊧𝒯C\models_{\mathcal{T}}C.

Note that 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn adds a non-ground theory lemma in general. This can then be instantiated by the rule Instantiate. If the added theory lemma is already ground, it can be instantiated with the empty substitution {}\{\}.

𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ∪{A};Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta\cup\{A\};\Gamma;N;G;k;\top)

given that A∉ΘA\notin\Theta and AA is a ground atom.

𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict

   (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) ⇒ICLF\quad\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

given that ⊧𝒯D\models_{\mathcal{T}}D, τ\tau is grounding for DD and D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma.

Just like in 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn, the conflict clause produced by 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict can be non-ground.

Explain

   (Θ,Γ1​L𝒯​Γ2,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}L^{\mathcal{T}}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ,Γ1​LC⋅σ​Γ2,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}L^{C\cdot\sigma}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

given that ⊧𝒯C\models_{\mathcal{T}}C, σ\sigma is grounding for CC, C​σ=C′∨LC\sigma=C^{\prime}\lor L and C′C^{\prime} is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

⊤\top is a short form for the conflict closure ⊤⋅{}\top\cdot\{\}, i.e., the rule Explain can be applied both in the model building and in the conflict analysis phase. Just like in 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, the reason can be non-ground. For each theory propagation on the trail, there exists a clause to apply Explain with, for example ¬Γ1∨L⋅{}\neg\Gamma_{1}\lor L\cdot\{\}, which is always valid in the theory by Lemma 5.

Finally, the following five rules are the conflict analysis rules.

Resolve

   (Θ,Γ1​LC⋅σ​Γ2,N,G,k,(D∨L′)⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}L^{C\cdot\sigma}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;(D\lor L^{\prime})\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ,Γ1​LC⋅σ​Γ2,N,G,k,resolve⁡(C⋅σ,D⋅τ,L′,L))(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}L^{C\cdot\sigma}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;\resolve(C\cdot\sigma,D\cdot\tau,L^{\prime},L))

given that L′​τ=comp⁡(L)L^{\prime}\tau=\comp(L).

The function resolve\resolve takes as arguments two variable disjoint closures C⋅σC\cdot\sigma and D⋅τD\cdot\tau, a literal L′L^{\prime} that does not occur in DD, may share variables with DD, but not with CC, and a ground literal LL such that L′​τ=comp⁡(L)L^{\prime}\tau=\comp(L). Let C=C′∨L1∨⋯∨LnC=C^{\prime}\lor L_{1}\lor\dots\lor L_{n} such that Li​σ=LL_{i}\sigma=L for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\} and LL does not occur in C′​σC^{\prime}\sigma. If μ=mgu⁡(comp⁡(L′),L1,…,Ln)\mu=\mgu(\comp(L^{\prime}),L_{1},\dots,L_{n}), then resolve⁡(C⋅σ,D⋅τ,L′,L)=(C′∨D)​μ⋅σ​τ\resolve(C\cdot\sigma,D\cdot\tau,L^{\prime},L)=(C^{\prime}\lor D)\mu\cdot\sigma\tau. In other words, the function resolve\resolve exhaustively factorizes LL in CC and computes a resolution inference between the two clauses.

The rule Resolve allows resolving any literal that is on the trail. This generality makes standard simplifications such as unit reduction possible. Additionally, it allows modeling conflict analysis procedures such as in standard CDCL with 1UIP learning [26] or in SCL [13] that work through the trail backwards, performing either Skip or Resolve for each encountered literal, as well as procedures like chronological backtracking [28, 27] that only resolve with a subsequence of the relevant literals on the trail.

Factorize

   (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,(D∨L∨L′)⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;(D\lor L\lor L^{\prime})\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,(D∨L)​η⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;(D\lor L)\eta\cdot\tau)

given that L​τ=L′​τL\tau=L^{\prime}\tau and η=mgu⁡(L,L′)\eta=\mgu(L,L^{\prime}).

The ground conflict clause does not change by applying Factorize. If the literal that Resolve is applied to can be factorized, then it does not disappear from the ground conflict clause after resolving. While the resulting ground conflict clause is the same regardless of whether a literal is exhaustively factorized before it is resolved or whether Resolve is applied multiple times, this is, in general, not true for the non-ground conflict clause [13, Example 3].

BacktrackClassic

   (Θ,Γ1​Kj​Γ2,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}K^{j}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ1LD⋅τ;N∪{D};G∪{D⋅τ};j−1;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}L^{D\cdot\tau};N\cup\{D\};G\cup\{D\cdot\tau\};j-1;\top)

given that D​τ=D′∨LD\tau=D^{\prime}\lor L, D′D^{\prime} is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1} and LL is propositionally undefined in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

BacktrackFOL

   (Θ,Γ1​Γ2,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2};N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ1;N∪{D};G∪{D⋅τ};j;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma_{1};N\cup\{D\};G\cup\{D\cdot\tau\};j;\top)

given that there is no grounding σ\sigma such that D​σD\sigma is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}, jj is the decision level of Γ1\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\Gamma_{2} contains a decision literal.

BacktrackCB

   (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau)

⇒ICLF\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}\quad (Θ;Γ′LD⋅τ;N∪{D};G∪{D⋅τ};j;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma^{\prime}L^{D\cdot\tau};N\cup\{D\};G\cup\{D\cdot\tau\};j;\top)

given that Γ′=cb⁡(Γ,D​τ,j)\Gamma^{\prime}=\cb(\Gamma,D\tau,j), D​τ=D′∨LD\tau=D^{\prime}\lor L, D′D^{\prime} is propositionally false in Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} and LL is propositionally undefined in Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}.

Here, CB stands for chronological backtracking [28, 27], an alternative backtracking scheme for CDCL that we adapt to ICLF in this paper. We now define the function cb\cb. To this end, given a trail Γ\Gamma, we first define the conflict graph as the directed acyclic graph whose nodes are the literals on the trail Γ\Gamma. Decision literals LkL^{k} and theory propagations L𝒯L^{\mathcal{T}} do not have any predecessors, and the predecessors of a propagation LC′⋅σL^{C^{\prime}\cdot\sigma} are the literals comp⁡(L′)\comp(L^{\prime}) for all L′∈C′​σL^{\prime}\in C^{\prime}\sigma with L′≠LL^{\prime}\neq L. If LL is a propagation (or an explained theory propagation), all of these predecessors are indeed literals on the trail. For each literal LL on the trail Γ\Gamma, we define reach⁡(L)\reach(L) as the set of literals that can be reached from LL in the conflict graph, including LL itself. By reach−1⁡(L)\reach^{-1}(L), we denote the set of literals that can reach LL in the conflict graph.

The arguments of the function cb\cb are a trail Γ\Gamma, a ground clause CC and a destination decision level jj that is smaller than the decision level of Γ\Gamma. Let Γ=Γ1​L′j+1​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}L^{\prime j+1}\Gamma_{2}. cb\cb is only applicable if the following three conditions are met. First, CC should be propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, i.e., for all L∈CL\in C, comp⁡(L)\comp(L) should be in Γ\Gamma. Second, |{comp⁡(L)∣L∈C}∩reach⁡(L′)|=1|\{\comp(L)\mid L\in C\}\cap\reach(L^{\prime})|=1, i.e., exactly one literal in CC should depend on the j+1j+1-st decision. Third, in ⋃L∈Creach−1⁡(comp⁡(L))∩Γ2\bigcup_{L\in C}\reach^{-1}(\comp(L))\cap\Gamma_{2}, there should be no literal annotated as a decision or theory propagation, i.e., no conflict literal should depend on a decision or theory propagation after L′L^{\prime} on the trail. Then, let C=C′∨L′′C=C^{\prime}\lor L^{\prime\prime} such that {comp⁡(L)∣L∈C′}∩reach⁡(L′)=∅\{\comp(L)\mid L\in C^{\prime}\}\cap\reach(L^{\prime})=\emptyset, i.e., L′′L^{\prime\prime} is the only literal in CC that depends on L′L^{\prime}. Further, let Γ3\Gamma_{3} be the subsequence of Γ2\Gamma_{2} that contains only the literals ⋃L∈C′reach−1⁡(comp⁡(L))∩Γ2\bigcup_{L\in C^{\prime}}\reach^{-1}(\comp(L))\cap\Gamma_{2}. It is crucial to note that Γ3\Gamma_{3} only contains propagations (and explained theory propagations), and that none of the literals in Γ3\Gamma_{3} was propagated from L′L^{\prime}. Then cb⁡(Γ,C,j)=Γ1​Γ3\cb(\Gamma,C,j)=\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{3}. By the aforementioned properties of Γ3\Gamma_{3}, all propagations in Γ3\Gamma_{3} are still justified in Γ1​Γ3\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{3} and C′C^{\prime} stays propositionally false in Γ1​Γ3\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{3}. Figure 1 illustrates this definition of the function cb\cb.

Definition 2.

A strategy for ICLF is called reasonable if the following are true:

  1. 1.

    The rule Conflict is preferred over the rules Decide, Propagate, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict.

  2. 2.

    No application of the rule Decide enables an immediate application of the rule Conflict.

  3. 3.

    If a conflict state is reached by the rule Conflict, then Resolve and Factorize are applied in such a way that the complement of the rightmost literal on the trail does not occur in the ground conflict clause anymore before applying any of the rules BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL or BacktrackCB.

These requirements do not cause any stuck states by Theorem 15. Although this does not affect correctness or termination, to avoid that previously resolved literals are reintroduced into the conflict clause, Resolve should be applied from right to left on the trail.

The goal of restricting the strategy is to learn only clauses that are non-redundant with respect to the current set of instantiations GG and a trail induced ordering [Definition 9]. Most SAT solvers implement CDCL with 1UIP learning [26]. In CDCL, the 1UIP clause is non-redundant because exhaustive propagation maintains the necessary invariants [41]. In ICLF, however, these invariants can be broken by theory rules and instantiations. For example, a newly instantiated clause may propagate with respect to an earlier trail prefix, making it possible for the 1UIP clause to be redundant. Moreover, for theory propagations and for literals propagated from them, the exact implying literals are not known before a theory explanation is computed, which may be expensive. For these reasons, 1UIP learning is not straightforward in our setting. Therefore, the restrictions of a reasonable strategy capture only what is needed for non-redundant learning and otherwise leave the conflict analysis rules general.

The following example shows ICLF in action modulo the theory of equality for the sake of simple theory reasoning. Of course, ICLF works modulo any suitable theory combination in the same way as CDCL(T). This run closely resembles quantifier instantiation combined with CDCL(T) and shows how ICLF can model this standard approach.

The following example shows how ICLF can learn non-ground clauses. Again, we work modulo the theory of equality to keep the theory reasoning simple.
