Of course, after the third propagation, Γ3\Gamma_{3} is already a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of G0G_{0}. However, consider a larger problem that contains the three clauses N​1N1, N​2N2, and N​3N3 among other clauses. In such a problem, another clause might have motivated the decision g⁡(a)≠ag(a)\neq a. A CDCL(T)-style approach with quantifier instantiation and ground 1UIP conflict analysis would learn the ground theory conflict clause h⁡(a)≠g⁡(a)∨h⁡(a)≠a∨g⁡(a)=ah(a)\neq g(a)\lor h(a)\neq a\lor g(a)=a from this conflict. By contrast, in this particular run, the generality of Resolve allows ICLF to resolve further with the three propagations and learn the more general clause g⁡(x4)=x4g(x_{4})=x_{4}. For these further resolution steps to yield the non-ground clause g⁡(x4)=x4g(x_{4})=x_{4}, the non-ground theory lemma x2≠x3∨x2≠x4∨x3=x4x_{2}\neq x_{3}\lor x_{2}\neq x_{4}\lor x_{3}=x_{4} is essential: starting from its ground instance instead, the same resolution steps would only yield the ground clause g⁡(a)=ag(a)=a. The learned non-ground clause can be useful later in the run: if g⁡(b)g(b) becomes relevant, it can be instantiated as g(x4)=x4⋅{x4↦b}g(x_{4})=x_{4}\cdot\{x_{4}\mapsto b\}, whereas the ground clause g⁡(a)=ag(a)=a carries no information about g⁡(b)g(b).

Next, we prove the correctness of ICLF and further properties, including non-redundant learning as well as termination and completeness under suitable restrictions. We start with invariants that are maintained by all ICLF rules. The proof is by induction on the length of the derivation, with a case distinction on the last applied rule.

Lemma 5 (Invariants).

Let (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) be a state reached from a start state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) by applying the rules of ICLF. Then the following hold:

  1. 1.

    For all C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G, it holds that C∈NC\in N.

  2. 2.

    atom⁡(Γ)∪atom⁡(clauses⁡(G))⊆Θ\atom(\Gamma)\cup\atom(\clauses(G))\subseteq\Theta and for all A∈ΘA\in\Theta, AA is a ground atom.

  3. 3.

    If Γ=Γ1​K​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K\Gamma_{2} then KK is propositionally undefined in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

  4. 4.

    If Γ=Γ1​LC⋅σ​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}L^{C\cdot\sigma}\Gamma_{2} then C​σC\sigma is ground, C​σ=C′∨LC\sigma=C^{\prime}\lor L, C′C^{\prime} is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1} and either C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G or ⊧𝒯C\models_{\mathcal{T}}C.

  5. 5.

    If Γ=Γ1​L𝒯​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}L^{\mathcal{T}}\Gamma_{2} then Γ1⊧𝒯L\Gamma_{1}\models_{\mathcal{T}}L.

  6. 6.

    Let k1,…,klk_{1},\dots,k_{l} be the annotations of decisions in Γ\Gamma. If there are no decisions, then k=0k=0; otherwise 1=k11=k_{1}, k=klk=k_{l} and for all i∈{2,…,l}i\in\{2,\dots,l\}, ki=ki−1+1k_{i}=k_{i-1}+1.

  7. 7.

    N′N^{\prime} and NN are equi-satisfiable in 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

  8. 8.

    If D≠⊤D\neq\top then D​τD\tau is ground, atom⁡(D​τ)⊆Θ\atom(D\tau)\subseteq\Theta and D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma.

  9. 9.

    clauses(G)⊧𝒯Dτ\clauses(G)\models_{\mathcal{T}}D\tau.

  10. 10.

    N⊧𝒯DN\models_{\mathcal{T}}D.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on the length of the derivation. In the start state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top), all properties obviously hold. The induction step is shown by a case distinction on the last applied rule. For readability, we only mention rules that modify any of the objects occurring in the respective property and skip cases in which the property obviously follows from the induction hypothesis. When we say that a rule asserts something, we mean that it follows from the premise and the patterns on the left side of the rule. To avoid confusion between variables used in this lemma and variables used in the rule definitions, we mark variables that refer to the rule definitions with a hat, e.g., C^\hat{C}.

Items 1 and 2: Instantiate asserts all of these properties for the newly added instance. ClauseDel asserts that Item 1 stays true after deleting the clause. AtomDel asserts that Item 2 stays true after deleting the atom. Decide asserts that Item 2 stays true after adding the literal to the trail. For Propagate, Item 2 for the newly added literal follows from the induction hypothesis because C^⋅σ^∈G\hat{C}\cdot\hat{\sigma}\in G. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate asserts that Item 2 stays true after adding the literal to the trail. BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL and BacktrackCB ensure Item 1 by adding D^\hat{D} to N^\hat{N} and D^⋅τ^\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau} to G^\hat{G} simultaneously. Item 2 follows from Item 8 of the induction hypothesis. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom asserts that Item 2 stays true after adding the atom to Θ\Theta.

Items 3, 4, 5 and 6: InstanceDel asserts that Item 4 stays true after deleting the instance. Decide asserts that Item 3 stays true after adding the literal to the trail. Item 6 follows from the induction hypothesis together with the level k+1k+1 that we assign to the added literal. Propagate asserts that Items 3 and 4 stay true after adding the literal to the trail. For Restart, all of these properties follow from the induction hypothesis because Γ^1\hat{\Gamma}_{1} is a prefix of Γ^\hat{\Gamma} and the decision level is set to be correct. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate asserts that Items 3 and 5 stay true after adding the literal to the trail. Explain asserts that Item 4 stays true after changing the annotation of the literal. BacktrackClassic and BacktrackCB assert that Items 3 and 4 stay true after adding the propagation from the learned clause. BacktrackClassic and BacktrackFOL assert that Item 6 stays true. The trail after BacktrackCB is Γ^1​Γ^3​L^D^⋅τ^\hat{\Gamma}_{1}\hat{\Gamma}_{3}\hat{L}^{\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau}}, where Γ^1​Γ^3=cb⁡(Γ^,D^​τ^,j^)\hat{\Gamma}_{1}\hat{\Gamma}_{3}=\cb(\hat{\Gamma},\hat{D}\hat{\tau},\hat{j}). As argued along the definition of the function cb\cb, Γ^3\hat{\Gamma}_{3} only contains propagations (and explained theory propagations), none of which depends on L′^\hat{L^{\prime}}, and all their implying literals are retained. Hence Item 5 follows from the induction hypothesis, and Item 4 follows from the induction hypothesis for the retained propagations and from the premise of BacktrackCB for the newly added propagation. Item 6 also stays true by the definition of the function cb\cb.

Item 7: ClauseDel asserts that this property stays true after deleting the clause. When applying 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn, the equi-satisfiability in 𝒯\mathcal{T} of N^\hat{N} and N^∪{C^}\hat{N}\cup\{\hat{C}\} follows from the fact that ⊧𝒯C^\models_{\mathcal{T}}\hat{C}. For BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL and BacktrackCB, this property follows from Item 10 of the induction hypothesis.

Items 8, 9 and 10: For all rules that leave a state with D⋅τ=⊤D\cdot\tau=\top, these properties are obviously true. For Conflict, Item 8 follows from Item 2 of the induction hypothesis and the premise of this rule. Item 9 is obvious and Item 10 follows from Item 1 of the induction hypothesis. For 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, Item 8 follows from the premise of this rule and Item 2 of the induction hypothesis; if D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, then all of its literals are contained in Γ\Gamma negatively. Items 9 and 10 are obvious because ⊧𝒯D\models_{\mathcal{T}}D. For Resolve, all of these properties follow from Items 1, 2, 4, 8, 9 and 10 of the induction hypothesis and the definition of the function resolve\resolve. Factorize trivially maintains Items 8 and 9 because D​τD\tau does not change by factorizing the literals L^\hat{L} and L′^\hat{L^{\prime}} with L^​τ^=L′^​τ^\hat{L}\hat{\tau}=\hat{L^{\prime}}\hat{\tau}. Item 10 follows from the induction hypothesis because (D^∨L^∨L′^)⊧(D^∨L^)​μ^(\hat{D}\lor\hat{L}\lor\hat{L^{\prime}})\models(\hat{D}\lor\hat{L})\hat{\mu}. ∎

The soundness of ICLF follows immediately from Items 7 and 10.

Theorem 6 (Soundness).

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊥)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\bot), then N′⊧𝒯⊥N^{\prime}\models_{\mathcal{T}}\bot.

Proof.

This follows from Items 7 and 10 of Lemma 5. ∎

The two previous statements hold regardless of the strategy used to apply the rules of ICLF. The following properties require the rules to be applied according to a reasonable strategy, as defined in Definition 2. We first show two invariants maintained by a reasonable strategy. The first invariant, Lemma 7, states that there is no propositional conflict for a proper trail prefix, and if the last literal on the trail is a decision, then there is no propositional conflict. This invariant is used to prove non-redundant learning with respect to GG in Theorem 11; it implies that, after conflict analysis, the learned clause is the only false clause for a suitable trail prefix [Lemma 10]. It also helps us show that whenever Conflict is applicable, the last literal on the trail is a propagation or a theory propagation whose complement occurs in the conflict clause [Lemma 8]. This is essential for satisfying the third requirement of a reasonable strategy, which requires resolving with the last literal on the trail before backtracking. The lemma is therefore used to show that there are no stuck states in Theorem 15.

Lemma 7.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ′;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma^{\prime};N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) using a reasonable strategy, then if Γ′=Γ​K\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma K, there is no C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, and if KK is a decision, then there is no C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ​K\Gamma K.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on the length of the derivation. The statement is obviously true for the start state. The induction step is shown by a case distinction on the last applied rule. For readability, we skip rules that do not modify the trail and do not insert into GG because for these rules, the statement trivially follows from the induction hypothesis.

Instantiate ensures in its premise that the new instance satisfies the condition. For Decide, this follows from the fact that a reasonable strategy is used: If there is a C⋅σC\cdot\sigma in GG such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, then Conflict would have been applicable instead of Decide, and if there is a C⋅σC\cdot\sigma in GG such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ​K\Gamma K, then Conflict would be applicable next, contradicting the fact that in a reasonable strategy, no application of the rule Decide enables an immediate application of the rule Conflict. For Propagate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate, we only have to argue about the case where an instance is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, and this follows from the same argument we used for Decide. For BacktrackClassic, for all clauses that were already contained in GG before applying this rule, the condition follows from the induction hypothesis because a suffix of the trail is deleted and then a decision is replaced by a propagation. For the learned clause, this follows from the premise of this rule. For BacktrackFOL, the argument is very similar, except that no propagation is added to the trail. For BacktrackCB, we actually need the third requirement of a reasonable strategy. During conflict analysis, the literals on the trail, NN and GG are not modified by any rule. If the conflict was reached by 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, then no instance in GG was propositionally false because otherwise, Conflict would have been applicable. If the conflict was reached by Conflict, then by the induction hypothesis, no instance in GG was propositionally false for a proper trail prefix. In a reasonable run, when BacktrackCB is applied, then the complement of the rightmost literal on the trail does not occur in the conflict clause. Thus, the rightmost literal on the trail is not contained in the subsequence of literals that is kept by the function cb\cb. From this, the statement follows for all instances that were previously contained in GG, and for the learned clause, it follows by the premise of this rule. ∎

Lemma 8.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) using a reasonable strategy and Conflict is applicable to this state with D⋅τ∈GD\cdot\tau\in G, then Γ=Γ1​K\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K, KK is not a decision literal and D​τD\tau is not propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

Proof.

By assumption, N′N^{\prime} does not contain the empty clause initially, and the empty clause is not valid in the theory, hence 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn cannot add it. The empty clause can also not be learned by any of the backtrack rules, so we can assume that NN does not contain the empty clause. Thus, by Item 1 of Lemma 5, GG does not contain the empty clause. From this, it follows that Γ≠ε\Gamma\neq\varepsilon, and the statement follows from Lemma 7. ∎

Now we are ready to show that ICLF learns only non-redundant clauses when a reasonable strategy is used. First, we define an ordering with respect to which the learned clauses are non-redundant.

Definition 9 (Trail Induced Ordering).

Given a trail Γ=L1​…​Ln\Gamma=L_{1}\dots L_{n}, we define the trail induced ordering ≺Γ\prec_{\Gamma} as a well-founded, total and strict ordering in which L1≺Γcomp(L1)≺ΓL2≺Γcomp(L2)≺Γ⋯≺ΓLn≺Γcomp(Ln)L_{1}\prec_{\Gamma}\comp(L_{1})\prec_{\Gamma}L_{2}\prec_{\Gamma}\comp(L_{2})\prec_{\Gamma}\dots\prec_{\Gamma}L_{n}\prec_{\Gamma}\comp(L_{n}) and all literals that are propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma are larger than comp⁡(Ln)\comp(L_{n}).

Lemma 10.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) using a reasonable strategy and BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL or BacktrackCB is applicable to this state following a reasonable strategy, then Γ=Γ1​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2}, D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1} and no clause in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}.

Proof.

If any backtrack rule is applicable to this state, then D∉{⊤,⊥}D\notin\{\top,\bot\}. This means that previously, either Conflict or 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict must have been applied, and that after the most recent application of Conflict or 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, only the rules Explain, Resolve and Factorize have been applied. Notice that none of these rules modifies the literals on the trail (Explain only modifies the annotations), and hence the literals on the trail are still the same as right before Conflict or 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict was applied. Moreover, none of these rules modifies Θ\Theta, NN, GG or kk. If the conflict state was reached by Conflict, then the complement of the rightmost literal on the trail does not occur in D​τD\tau because a reasonable strategy was used. Hence, by Item 8 of Lemma 5, it follows that Γ=Γ1​K\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K and D​τD\tau is false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Now, the claim follows from Lemma 7. If the conflict state was reached by 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, then there is no C⋅σC\cdot\sigma in GG that is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma because otherwise, Conflict would have been applicable instead, and the claim follows. ∎

Theorem 11 (Non-Redundant Learning).

Whenever ICLF learns a ground clause (using BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL or BacktrackCB) in a reasonable run, this clause is non-redundant with respect to the current set of ground instances and the trail induced ordering.

Proof.

Assume that ICLF is in the state (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) that BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL or BacktrackCB is applicable to. By Lemma 10, Γ=Γ1​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2}, D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1} and no clause in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. This means that in particular, all literals of D​τD\tau are propositionally defined in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Consider the set clauses(G)⪯ΓDτ\clauses(G)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}. All literals of the clauses in this set must be propositionally defined in Γ1\Gamma_{1} as well because they are all ⪯ΓDτ\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau. As no clause in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}, it holds that Γ1⊧clauses(G)⪯ΓDτ\Gamma_{1}\models\clauses(G)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}. It follows that clauses(G)⪯ΓDτ⊧̸Dτ\clauses(G)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}\not\models D\tau because otherwise, by transitivity of entailment, it would follow that Γ1⊧D​τ\Gamma_{1}\models D\tau, contradicting the fact that D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Hence, D​τD\tau is non-redundant with respect to clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) and the trail induced ordering ≺Γ\prec_{\Gamma}. ∎

The non-ground learned clause DD, however, can be redundant with respect to NN and the trail-induced ordering ≺Γ\prec_{\Gamma}. This can happen, for example, if there is an instance of a clause in NN that is propositionally false for a trail prefix, but that is not contained in GG; one such case is shown in Example 12. Theorem 18 shows that if a stronger strategy, called first-order aware strategy [Definition 17], is followed, then the non-ground learned clause DD is also non-redundant with respect to NN. Moreover, Theorem 19 shows that following a first-order aware strategy does not cause any stuck states.

Example 12.

Consider the clause set

N0={(N1)P(x0),(N2)P(x1)∨R(x1),(N3)Q(x2)∨¬R(x2)}.\displaystyle N_{0}=\{(N1)~P(x_{0}),~~~~~(N2)~P(x_{1})\lor R(x_{1}),~~~~~(N3)~Q(x_{2})\lor\neg R(x_{2})\}.
(∅;ε;N0;∅;0;⊤)\displaystyle(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N_{0};\emptyset;0;\top)
⇒ICLFInstantiate ×2\displaystyle\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}~~~~~~~~~~~~~}^{\text{Instantiate $\times 2$}}\quad (Θ0;ε;N0;G0;0;⊤)\displaystyle(\Theta_{0};\varepsilon;N_{0};G_{0};0;\top)
Here, Θ0={P⁡(a),R⁡(a),Q⁡(a)}\Theta_{0}=\{P(a),R(a),Q(a)\} and G0={(G1)P(x1)∨R(x1)⋅{x1↦a},(G2)Q(x2)∨¬R(x2)⋅{x2↦a}}G_{0}=\{(G1)~P(x_{1})\lor R(x_{1})\cdot\{x_{1}\mapsto a\},(G2)~Q(x_{2})\lor\neg R(x_{2})\cdot\{x_{2}\mapsto a\}\}.
⇒ICLFDecide ×2\displaystyle\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}~~~~~~~~~~~~~}^{\text{Decide $\times 2$}}\quad (Θ0;¬P(a)1¬Q(a)2;N0;G0;2;⊤)\displaystyle(\Theta_{0};\neg P(a)^{1}\neg Q(a)^{2};N_{0};G_{0};2;\top)
⇒ICLFPropagate\displaystyle\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}~~~~~~~~~~~~~}^{\text{Propagate}}\quad (Θ0;¬P(a)1¬Q(a)2R(a)(G​1);N0;G0;2;⊤)\displaystyle(\Theta_{0};\neg P(a)^{1}\neg Q(a)^{2}R(a)^{(G1)};N_{0};G_{0};2;\top)
⇒ICLFConflict\displaystyle\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}~~~~~~~~~~~~~}^{\text{Conflict}}\quad (Θ0;¬P(a)1¬Q(a)2R(a)(G​1);N0;G0;2;Q(x2)∨¬R(x2)⋅{x2↦a})\displaystyle(\Theta_{0};\neg P(a)^{1}\neg Q(a)^{2}R(a)^{(G1)};N_{0};G_{0};2;Q(x_{2})\lor\neg R(x_{2})\cdot\{x_{2}\mapsto a\})
⇒ICLFResolve\displaystyle\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}~~~~~~~~~~~~~}^{\text{Resolve}}\quad (Θ0;¬P(a)1¬Q(a)2R(a)(G​1);N0;G0;2;P(x2)∨Q(x2)⋅{x2↦a})\displaystyle(\Theta_{0};\neg P(a)^{1}\neg Q(a)^{2}R(a)^{(G1)};N_{0};G_{0};2;P(x_{2})\lor Q(x_{2})\cdot\{x_{2}\mapsto a\})

The clause P⁡(x2)∨Q⁡(x2)P(x_{2})\lor Q(x_{2}) that can now be learned is non-redundant with respect to G0G_{0}, but redundant with respect to N0N_{0} due to the clause P⁡(x0)P(x_{0}). This also illustrates the difference between a reasonable and a first-order aware strategy. A first-order aware strategy prevents the decision ¬P⁡(a)\neg P(a) since it makes an instance of P⁡(x0)∈N0P(x_{0})\in N_{0} propositionally false, whereas a reasonable strategy allows this decision because P⁡(a)∉clauses⁡(G0)P(a)\notin\clauses(G_{0}).

Corollary 13.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) using a reasonable strategy, then there are no two C⋅σ,C′⋅σ′∈GC\cdot\sigma,C^{\prime}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\in G such that C⋅σ≠C′⋅σ′C\cdot\sigma\neq C^{\prime}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}, but C​σ=C′​σ′C\sigma=C^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on the length of the derivation. The statement is obviously true for the start state. For the induction step, we only have to consider rules that insert instances into GG. Instantiate asserts this property in its premise, and for the backtrack rules, it follows from Theorem 11. ∎

Without restrictions, termination cannot be expected for ICLF: Instantiate may generate infinitely many ground instances, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn may add infinitely many theory lemmas, and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom may add arbitrary ground atoms. Even ground reasoning on a fixed set of ground instances may diverge due to Restart and InstanceDel, the latter being analogous to Forget in CDCL(T). We therefore prove termination when these rules are applied only finitely often. Such restrictions are standard in related settings. For example, SCL restricts trail literals to be smaller than a fixed bound β\beta, thereby obtaining only finitely many relevant instances [13]. In CDCL, restarts can be performed with increasing periodicity to ensure termination [30]. The following theorem states the corresponding termination condition for ICLF.

Theorem 14 (Termination).

If ICLF is executed from a start state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) using a reasonable strategy, and the rules Instantiate, InstanceDel, Restart, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn, and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom are applied only finitely often, then it terminates.

Proof.

Assume (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau). It is enough to show that there is no infinite sequence of reasonable rule applications from this state if the rules Instantiate, InstanceDel, Restart, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom are not applied. For this purpose, we define a function numT⁡(Γ^)\numT(\hat{\Gamma}) that counts the number of 𝒯\mathcal{T} annotations on a trail Γ^\hat{\Gamma}, and a function multiGround⁡(D^⋅τ^)\multiGround(\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau}) that maps closures to the multiset multiGround(D^⋅τ^)={|Lτ^∣L∈D^|}\multiGround(\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau})=\{|L\hat{\tau}\mid L\in\hat{D}|\}. We now associate states (Θ^,Γ^,N^,G^,k^,D^⋅τ^)(\hat{\Theta};\hat{\Gamma};\hat{N};\hat{G};\hat{k};\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau}) with the five tuple

(4|Θ^|−|clauses⁡(G^)|,|N^|,|Θ^|−|Γ^|,numT⁡(Γ^),multiGround⁡(D^⋅τ^)).\displaystyle\left(4^{\big|\hat{\Theta}\big|}-\big|\clauses(\hat{G})\big|,~~\big|\hat{N}\big|,~~\big|\hat{\Theta}\big|-\big|\hat{\Gamma}\big|,~~\numT\big(\hat{\Gamma}\big),~~\multiGround(\hat{D}\cdot\hat{\tau})\right).

By Items 2 and 3 of Lemma 5, the first and third component are natural numbers. For the second and fourth component, it is obvious that they are natural numbers. The fifth component is compared by the multiset extension of the trail induced ordering ≺Γ^\prec_{\hat{\Gamma}}, which is well-founded. We assume that multiGround⁡(⊤)\multiGround(\top) is maximal in this ordering. It suffices to show that each of the remaining rules decreases this five tuple with respect to the lexicographic ordering. The fact that the trail Γ^\hat{\Gamma}, and hence the trail induced ordering ≺Γ^\prec_{\hat{\Gamma}}, are not constant is not a problem, as changes of the trail Γ^\hat{\Gamma} always coincide with a decrease in an earlier component.

For readability, we only write for each rule which component it decreases, and omit the sentence that the earlier components remain unchanged. ClauseDel decreases the second component. AtomDel decreases the first component. Decide and Propagate decrease the third component. Conflict decreases the fifth component. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate decreases the third component. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict decreases the fifth component. Explain decreases the fourth component. Resolve and Factorize decrease the fifth component. By Theorem 11, BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL and BacktrackCB decrease the first component. ∎

Theorem 15 (No Stuck States).

Let (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) be a state reached by ICLF from a start state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) using a reasonable strategy. Then either D=⊥D=\bot, or D=⊤D=\top and Γ\Gamma is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G), or a rule from the set {\{Decide, Propagate, Conflict, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, Explain, Resolve, B}\} is applicable following a reasonable strategy, where B is any of the rules BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL or BacktrackCB.

Proof.

First assume that D=⊤D=\top, but Γ\Gamma is not a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G). If there is an instance C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, then Conflict is applicable. If there is some A∈ΘA\in\Theta such that AA is propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma, then either Propagate or Decide are applicable with AA or ¬A\neg A. Otherwise, by Item 2 of Lemma 5, all instances in GG are propositionally true, which means that by our assumption, Γ\Gamma is not 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable. It follows that 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict is applicable, for instance with ¬Γ⋅{}\neg\Gamma\cdot\{\}.

Now assume that D∉{⊤,⊥}D\notin\{\top,\bot\}. By Item 5 of Lemma 5, for any literal LL on the trail such that Γ=Γ1​L𝒯​Γ2\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}L^{\mathcal{T}}\Gamma_{2}, Explain is applicable, for instance with ¬Γ1∨L\neg\Gamma_{1}\lor L. Hence, we can assume that we can apply Resolve on any literal on the trail that is not a decision. By Item 8 of Lemma 5, the complements of all literals in D​τD\tau are on the trail. We now show that for each backtrack rule, there exists an approach to be able to apply it. If the respective backtrack rule is not applicable due to the restrictions of the reasonable strategy, then Resolve can be applied with the rightmost literal on the trail, whose complement in this case occurs in the conflict clause by Lemma 8. It is possible to resolve with this rightmost literal on the trail until its complement does not occur in the conflict clause anymore by Item 4 of Lemma 5 and Theorem 14. If BacktrackClassic is not applicable, then the rightmost complement of a literal in D​τD\tau on the trail is not a decision, so Resolve can be applied with it. Following this process, either ⊥\bot will be derived or BacktrackClassic becomes applicable eventually. The same strategy works for BacktrackCB because if the rightmost complement of a literal in D​τD\tau is a decision L′j+1L^{\prime j+1}, then all conditions for the applicability of cb\cb are met. If there is no decision on the trail Γ\Gamma, then ⊥\bot can be derived by applying Resolve several times. Otherwise, BacktrackFOL is always applicable with Γ1=ε\Gamma_{1}=\varepsilon. ∎

In full generality, completeness cannot be expected for arbitrary theories and theory combinations, for example for linear arithmetic combined with uninterpreted function symbols [2, 40, 24]. Nevertheless, Theorems 14 and 15 imply completeness whenever a finite 𝒯\mathcal{T}-unsatisfiable set of ground instances is available.

Corollary 16 (Completeness).

Let NN be a clause set and S⊆gnd⁡(N)S\subseteq\gnd(N) be finite and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-unsatisfiable. Then ICLF can derive ⊥\bot.

Proof.

We first apply Instantiate with all clauses in SS, which is possible by the definition of gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N) and the fact that the trail is empty in the start state. Now, the rules Decide, Propagate, Conflict, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, Explain, Resolve and BacktrackClassic are applied exhaustively following a reasonable strategy. None of these rules deletes clauses from GG. By Theorem 14, applying these rules exhaustively terminates. By Theorem 15, ⊥\bot must have been derived because S⊆clauses⁡(G)S\subseteq\clauses(G) is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-unsatisfiable, so there cannot be a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G). ∎

Definition 17.

A strategy for ICLF is called first-order aware if it is reasonable and the following are true:

  1. 1.

    If Instantiate is applicable with a propositionally false instance, then this is always preferred over applying 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict.

  2. 2.

    At no point during the run is there a clause in the clause set that has an instance that is propositionally false for a proper trail prefix.

  3. 3.

    Whenever the rightmost literal on the trail is a decision, no clause in the clause set has an instance that is propositionally false on the trail.

Theorem 18.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) using a first-order aware strategy and one of the rules BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL and BacktrackCB is applicable to this state following a first-order aware strategy, then the clause DD added to NN by the respective backtrack rule is non-redundant with respect to NN and the trail induced ordering ≺Γ\prec_{\Gamma}.

Proof.

We show the non-redundancy of DD by showing that D​τ∈gnd⁡(D)D\tau\in\gnd(D) is non-redundant with respect to gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N). Consider the set gnd(N)⪯ΓDτ\gnd(N)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}. Analogously to the proof of Lemma 10, we distinguish whether the conflict state was reached by Conflict or 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict.

First consider the case that the conflict state was reached by the rule Conflict. Then Γ=Γ1​K\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K and D​τD\tau is propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Due to the fact that a first-order aware strategy is used, no clause in gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N) can be propositionally false in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Nevertheless, all literals of the clauses in gnd(N)⪯ΓDτ\gnd(N)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau} are propositionally defined in Γ1\Gamma_{1}, which means that Γ1⊧gnd(N)⪯ΓDτ\Gamma_{1}\models\gnd(N)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}, from which, analogously to the proof of Theorem 11, it follows that gnd(N)⪯ΓDτ⊧̸Dτ\gnd(N)^{\preceq_{\Gamma}D\tau}\not\models D\tau, hence, DD is non-redundant with respect to NN and ≺Γ\prec_{\Gamma}.

Now consider the case that the conflict state was reached by the rule 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict. We argue that no clause in gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N) can be propositionally false in Γ\Gamma. From this, the claim follows analogously to the case that the conflict state was reached by Conflict. Clearly, Γ=Γ1​K\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}K. If KK is a propagation or theory propagation, then no clause in gnd⁡(N)\gnd(N) can be propositionally false in Γ\Gamma because otherwise Conflict, possibly after Instantiate, would have been applied in a first-order aware strategy instead of 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict. If KK is a decision, then this follows directly from the fact that a first-order aware strategy is used. ∎

Theorem 19.

If (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLF∗(Θ;Γ;N;G;k;D⋅τ)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) using a first-order aware strategy, then either D=⊥D=\bot, or D=⊤D=\top, Γ\Gamma is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) and no instance of a clause in NN is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, or a rule from the set {\{Instantiate, Decide, Propagate, Conflict, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, Explain, Resolve, BacktrackFOL}\} is applicable following a first-order aware strategy. Additionally, Instantiate only has to be applied with instances whose atoms are already contained in Θ\Theta.

Proof.

It is obvious that the start state is valid in a first-order aware strategy. First assume that D=⊤D=\top, but Γ\Gamma is not a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) or there is an instance of a clause in NN that is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma. Further assume that there is a C∈NC\in N and a grounding σ\sigma such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma. If C​σ∈clauses⁡(G)C\sigma\in\clauses(G), then Conflict is applicable. Otherwise, due to the fact that a first-order aware strategy is used, the rightmost literal in Γ\Gamma is a propagation or theory propagation, so Instantiate is applicable. Due to the fact that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, all of its atoms are indeed contained in Θ\Theta by Item 2 of Lemma 5. Now consider the case that no instance of a clause in NN is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma. If there is some A∈ΘA\in\Theta that is propositionally undefined in Γ\Gamma, then either Propagate or Decide are applicable with AA or ¬A\neg A. In the case of Propagate, it is not possible that the first-order aware strategy is violated because by assumption, there is no propositionally false instance in Γ\Gamma, which becomes the longest proper trail prefix after applying Propagate. If the application of Decide would cause a propositionally false instance, then either this instance can be used to propagate the complement instead, or Instantiate can be applied instead. Again, clearly all atoms of this instance are already contained in Θ\Theta. If all A∈ΘA\in\Theta are propositionally defined in Γ\Gamma, then all instances in GG must be propositionally true, which means that by our assumption, Γ\Gamma is not 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict can be applied in this case, for example, with ¬Γ⋅{}\neg\Gamma\cdot\{\}. This does not violate the first-order aware strategy because by assumption, no instance is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma.

Now assume that D∉{⊤,⊥}D\notin\{\top,\bot\}. Analogously to the proof of Theorem 15, either ⊥\bot can be derived or a state can be reached in which BacktrackFOL is applicable according to a reasonable strategy. This is because none of the rules Explain, Resolve and Factorize modifies the literals on the trail or the clause set. Now BacktrackFOL can be applied to go back to any trail prefix Γ1\Gamma_{1} for which DD has no false instance and such that the removed suffix contains a decision; in particular, Γ1=ε\Gamma_{1}=\varepsilon is possible. ∎

It should be noted that although following a first-order aware strategy does not cause any stuck states [Theorem 19], it limits the applicability of some rules. For instance, Propagate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate cannot be applied if there is an uninstantiated false instance; instead, this false instance has to be instantiated. Additionally, Decide cannot be applied if doing so would make some instance false. In this sense, the requirements of a first-order aware strategy in ICLF are very similar to the requirements of a regular run in SCL(FOL) [13]. Moreover, the first-order aware strategy also restricts the applicability of 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn. If a clause that has a propositionally false instance should be added by 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn, Restart can first be used to go back to a point on the trail at which no instance is propositionally false. Beyond that, while detecting conflicts and propagations with respect to ground clause sets such as GG is straightforward, both tasks are NP-complete in the worst case with respect to first-order clause sets such as NN; nevertheless, the recent lifting of the two-watched literal scheme to first-order logic shows that such clause sets can still be handled efficiently in practice [8].

4 Simulation of Other Calculi

In this section, we show that ICLF can simulate various other calculi. To avoid confusion, we mark variables from the simulated calculi with an overline, e.g., N¯\overline{N}, and refer to variables from ICLF without any overlines, e.g., by NN.

First, we show that ICLF can simulate SCL(FOL) [13]. This means that we associate each possible SCL(FOL) state with a set of ICLF states. Then, we show that for each state in a given SCL(FOL) run, we can find an associated ICLF state and ICLF rule applications between these states. The simulation is linear in the sense that for each SCL(FOL) rule application, only a constant number of ICLF rule applications has to be performed. SCL(FOL) is an algorithm for first-order logic without equality, so we assume 𝒯\mathcal{T} to be the free theory, i.e., the theory that contains all Σ\Sigma-algebras. For SCL(FOL), we write the status closure as D¯⋅τ¯\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}, assuming that ⊤=⊤⋅{}\top=\top\cdot\{\} and ⊥=⊥⋅{}\bot=\bot\cdot\{\}, just as we do for ICLF. Let ≺B\prec_{B} be a well-founded, total and strict ordering on ground atoms such that for any ground atom AA, there are only finitely many ground atoms A′A^{\prime} with A′≺BAA^{\prime}\prec_{B}A. ≺B\prec_{B} is lifted to literals by comparing the respective atoms and to clauses by its multiset extension.

Definition 20.

We say that an ICLF state (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) is associated with a given SCL(FOL) state (Γ¯,N¯,U¯,β¯,k¯,D¯⋅τ¯)(\overline{\Gamma};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{\beta};\overline{k};\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}) if all of the following hold:

  1. 1.

    D⋅τ=D¯⋅τ¯D\cdot\tau=\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}.

  2. 2.

    For all A∈ΘA\in\Theta, A≺Bβ¯A\prec_{B}\overline{\beta} and there is an atom A′∈atom⁡(N)A^{\prime}\in\atom(N) such that AA is a ground instance of A′A^{\prime}.

  3. 3.

    N=N¯∪U¯N=\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}.

  4. 4.

    k≥k¯k\geq\overline{k}. If D¯⋅τ¯=⊤\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\top, then k=k¯k=\overline{k}.

  5. 5.

    If Γ=K1​…​Kn\Gamma=K_{1}\dots K_{n} and Γ¯=K¯1​…​K¯n¯\overline{\Gamma}=\overline{K}_{1}\dots\overline{K}_{\overline{n}}, then n≥n¯n\geq\overline{n} and for all i∈{1,…,n¯}i\in\{1,\dots,\overline{n}\}, KiK_{i} and K¯i\overline{K}_{i} match. By match, we mean that either Ki=K¯i=LjK_{i}=\overline{K}_{i}=L^{j} or that Ki=LC⋅σK_{i}=L^{C\cdot\sigma}, K¯i=LC¯⋅σ¯\overline{K}_{i}=L^{\overline{C}\cdot\overline{\sigma}} and C¯⋅σ¯\overline{C}\cdot\overline{\sigma} is the result of exhaustively factorizing LL in C⋅σC\cdot\sigma. If D¯⋅τ¯=⊤\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\top, then n=n¯n=\overline{n}.

Theorem 21 (ICLF Simulates SCL(FOL)).

Let N′N^{\prime} be a first-order clause set and β′\beta^{\prime} be a ground literal. Then for any regular SCL(FOL) run

(ε;N′;∅;β′;0;⊤)=S0⇒SCL(FOL)S1⇒SCL(FOL)…⇒SCL(FOL)Sm,(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;\beta^{\prime};0;\top)=S_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(FOL)}}^{\text{}}S_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(FOL)}}^{\text{}}\dots\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(FOL)}}^{\text{}}S_{m},

there exists a reasonable ICLF run

(∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)=T0⇒ICLF≤3T1⇒ICLF≤3…⇒ICLF≤3Tm(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)=T_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 3$}}T_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 3$}}\dots\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 3$}}T_{m}

such that for all i∈{0,…,m}i\in\{0,\dots,m\}, TiT_{i} is associated with SiS_{i}. Here, ⇒ICLF≤3\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 3$}} means that at most three ICLF rules are applied to reach the following state. Only the ICLF rules Instantiate, InstanceDel, Decide, Propagate, Conflict, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom, Resolve, Factorize and BacktrackFOL are needed.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on mm. The start state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) of ICLF is obviously associated with (ε;N′;∅;β′;0;⊤)(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;\beta^{\prime};0;\top), the start state of SCL(FOL). Now let Sm′=(Γ¯,N¯,U¯,β¯,k¯,D¯⋅τ¯)S_{m^{\prime}}=(\overline{\Gamma};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{\beta};\overline{k};\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}) and Tm′=(Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)T_{m^{\prime}}=(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau). We show the induction step by a case distinction on the SCL(FOL) rule that is applied to reach Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1} from Sm′S_{m^{\prime}}. For readability, we do not mention properties that neither the applied SCL(FOL) rule nor any of the applied ICLF rules change, as these trivially follow from the induction hypothesis. We first argue that the first two requirements of a reasonable strategy in ICLF do not restrict the simulation. If the rule Conflict is applicable in ICLF, then it is also applicable for any associated SCL(FOL) state because the first-order clause that the conflict clause is an instance of is also contained in the SCL(FOL) state by Item 1 of Lemma 5 and the fact that N=N¯∪U¯N=\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}. A regular SCL(FOL) run follows the same requirements about preferring Conflict over Propagate and Decide and Decide not enabling Conflict as a reasonable ICLF run. Hence, whenever Propagate and Decide can be applied in a regular SCL(FOL) run, they can also be applied in a reasonable ICLF run.

Propagate: Let C∨LC\lor L be the clause used for propagation and σ\sigma be the grounding such that L​σL\sigma is the propagated literal. Since C∨L∈(N¯∪U¯)C\lor L\in(\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}), C∨L∈NC\lor L\in N. If (C∨L)⋅σ∈G(C\lor L)\cdot\sigma\in G, then Propagate can be applied in ICLF right away, otherwise Instantiate has to be applied first. If Instantiate is not applicable because (C∨L)​σ∈clauses⁡(G)(C\lor L)\sigma\in\clauses(G), then InstanceDel can be applied with this other instance because by Item 4 of Lemma 5, this other instance cannot be an annotation of a literal on the trail because otherwise, Propagate would not be applicable with (C∨L)​σ(C\lor L)\sigma. By Corollary 13, there is at most one such instance in GG that has to be deleted. It is not possible that the new instance is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma because the literals in Γ\Gamma and Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} are the same and Conflict would have been applied in a regular SCL(FOL) run instead. The atoms added to Θ\Theta by Instantiate are smaller than β¯\overline{\beta} because (C∨L)σ≺B{β¯}(C\lor L)\sigma\prec_{B}\{\overline{\beta}\} by the premise of SCL(FOL) Propagate, and they are obviously ground instances of atoms in atom⁡(N)=atom⁡(N¯∪U¯)\atom(N)=\atom(\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}). The propagated literal is L​σL\sigma in both cases and the annotation in SCL(FOL) is the result of exhaustively factorizing the annotation in ICLF.

Decide: Let LL be a literal occurring in N¯∪U¯\overline{N}\cup\overline{U} and L​σL\sigma be the decided literal. If atom⁡(L​σ)∈Θ\atom(L\sigma)\in\Theta, then Decide can be applied in ICLF right away, otherwise 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom can be applied with atom⁡(L​σ)\atom(L\sigma) first. The atom added to Θ\Theta is smaller than β¯\overline{\beta} and a ground instance of an atom in atom⁡(N)=atom⁡(N¯∪U¯)\atom(N)=\atom(\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}) by the premise of SCL(FOL) Decide. Both SCL(FOL) Decide and ICLF Decide add the same ground literal L​σL\sigma with the same annotation k+1=k¯+1k+1=\overline{k}+1 to the trail.

Conflict: Let C∈N¯∪U¯C\in\overline{N}\cup\overline{U} be the conflicting clause and σ\sigma be the grounding for CC. If C⋅σC\cdot\sigma is contained in GG, then Conflict can be applied in ICLF immediately, otherwise Instantiate has to be applied first. If Instantiate is not applicable because C​σ∈clauses⁡(G)C\sigma\in\clauses(G), then InstanceDel must be applied with the other instance first, which is possible because C​σC\sigma is false in Γ\Gamma, so the other instance cannot be an annotation of a literal on the trail. By Corollary 13, there is at most one such instance in GG that has to be deleted. When Conflict is applicable in a regular SCL(FOL) run, then the rightmost literal on the trail is a propagation that occurs negatively in the conflict clause [13, Lemma 11]. Hence, by Item 3 of Lemma 5, the remaining requirements of Instantiate are met. After applying Conflict, the conflict closures in SCL(FOL) and ICLF are the same.

Skip: Tm′T_{m^{\prime}} is also associated with Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}, so no ICLF rule has to be applied.

Factorize: The SCL(FOL) rule Factorize can be simulated by the ICLF rule Factorize.

Resolve: The SCL(FOL) rule Resolve can be simulated by the ICLF rule Resolve. Propagation annotations in SCL(FOL) are already exhaustively factorized, whereas ICLF factorizes them in Resolve.

Backtrack: The SCL(FOL) rule Backtrack can be simulated by the ICLF rule BacktrackFOL. As the conflict clauses are the same, the SCL(FOL) trail is a prefix of the ICLF trail in the state that Backtrack is applied to and SCL(FOL) skips over a decision, ICLF can go back to the same point on the trail that SCL(FOL) goes back to. What is left to argue is that BacktrackFOL can be applied in a reasonable strategy. In the simulation, we use the ICLF rule Conflict only when SCL(FOL) uses its Conflict rule, and whenever SCL(FOL) resolves, ICLF also resolves in the simulation. Since in SCL(FOL), the rightmost literal on the trail is always resolved exhaustively during conflict resolution [13, Lemma 11], BacktrackFOL is applicable in a reasonable strategy in ICLF whenever Backtrack is applicable in SCL(FOL).

Grow: As the new bound is ≺B\prec_{B}-larger than the old bound β¯\overline{\beta}, Tm′T_{m^{\prime}} is also associated with Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}, so no ICLF rule has to be applied. ∎

A further lemma in the appendix shows that if SCL(FOL) reaches a stuck state, then the associated ICLF state reached in the corresponding simulation is also stuck according to a suitable definition of stuckness [Lemma 30].

SCL(FOL) has been shown to simulate non-redundant ground superposition [12, 10]. Since ICLF simulates SCL(FOL), this result also transfers to ICLF. For ICLF, however, we can show a stronger result: it can simulate any resolution inference that does not yield a tautology, provided that neither parent clause becomes tautological under the most general unifier of the resolved literals. If a parent clause does become tautological, the resolvent is already subsumed by the other parent clause. This does not contradict the non-redundancy guarantee for reasonable strategies, because learned clauses are guaranteed to be non-redundant only with respect to GG. Since ICLF does not force all clauses to be instantiated, a clause that is redundant with respect to NN may still be non-redundant with respect to GG.

Remark 22 (ICLF Simulates Resolution).

Let (Θ;Γ;N;G;k;⊤)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;\top) be an ICLF state reached in a reasonable run, and let C1∨L1,C2∨L2∈NC_{1}\lor L_{1},C_{2}\lor L_{2}\in N be such that L1L_{1} and comp⁡(L2)\comp(L_{2}) are unifiable. Let μ=mgu⁡(L1,comp⁡(L2))\mu=\mgu(L_{1},\comp(L_{2})). If the resolvent of the clauses is not a tautology and neither parent clause becomes tautological under μ\mu, then ICLF can learn it or a clause subsuming it by following a reasonable strategy as follows. We first apply Restart with Γ1=ε\Gamma_{1}=\varepsilon to empty the trail, and then InstanceDel on all instances in GG to empty the set of ground instances. Next, we apply Instantiate with (C1∨L1)⋅(μ​σ)(C_{1}\lor L_{1})\cdot(\mu\sigma) and (C2∨L2)⋅(μ​σ)(C_{2}\lor L_{2})\cdot(\mu\sigma), where we pick σ\sigma such that no two atoms A1,A2∈atom⁡(C1∪C2∪{L1,L2})A_{1},A_{2}\in\atom(C_{1}\cup C_{2}\cup\{L_{1},L_{2}\}) with A1​μ≠A2​μA_{1}\mu\neq A_{2}\mu become equal. This can, for example, be achieved by instantiating all variables with different fresh constants. Then, we decide the complements of all literals except for L1​μ​σL_{1}\mu\sigma and L2​μ​σL_{2}\mu\sigma. This is possible because the resolvent of the clauses is not a tautology, because neither parent clause is tautological under μ\mu, and because of the way we chose σ\sigma. It also does not contradict the reasonable strategy because neither of the two ground instances can be false at this point. We then propagate L1​μ​σL_{1}\mu\sigma and apply Conflict with (C2∨L2)⋅(μ​σ)(C_{2}\lor L_{2})\cdot(\mu\sigma). Resolving exhaustively with L1​μ​σL_{1}\mu\sigma yields the desired resolvent, or, due to exhaustive factorization, a clause subsuming it. The derived clause is either ⊥\bot or can be learned using BacktrackClassic.

Now, we show that ICLF can simulate clause learning in SCL(T) [11]. Unlike in the simulation of SCL(FOL), we do not simulate every rule application. Instead, we simulate the sequence of rule applications that leads to the application of Conflict and show that ICLF can learn the same clause that SCL(T) learns. We assume that a constrained clause Λ|C\Lambda\parallel C is just a different notation for the clause ¬Λ∨C\neg\Lambda\lor C and note the status closure for SCL(T) as D¯⋅τ¯\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}, assuming that ⊤=⊤⋅{}\top=\top\cdot\{\}. Let N′N^{\prime} be a pure, abstracted clause set according to the requirements of SCL(T) and B′B^{\prime} be a finite sequence of constants of background sorts.

Definition 23.

We say that an ICLF state (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) is weakly associated with a given SCL(T) state (M¯,N¯,U¯,B¯,k¯,D¯⋅τ¯)(\overline{M};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{B};\overline{k};\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}) if N=N¯∪U¯N=\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}, D⋅τ=D¯⋅τ¯D\cdot\tau=\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}, and the background literals in Γ\Gamma form a prefix of Γ\Gamma. It is called associated if additionally, the set of literals in M¯\overline{M} is a subset of the set of literals in Γ\Gamma, the foreground literals in M¯\overline{M} form a subsequence of Γ\Gamma, and for all propagations LC¯⋅σ¯L^{\overline{C}\cdot\overline{\sigma}} in M¯\overline{M}, the corresponding literal LL in Γ\Gamma is annotated with a closure C⋅σC\cdot\sigma such that C¯⋅σ¯\overline{C}\cdot\overline{\sigma} is the result of exhaustively factorizing LL in C⋅σC\cdot\sigma, and for all decisions LkL^{k} in M¯\overline{M}, the corresponding literal LL in Γ\Gamma is also a decision.

Theorem 24 (Simulation of Conflict).

For any regular SCL(T) run

(ε;N′;∅;B′;0;⊤)⇒SCL(T)∗S0⇒SCL(T)∗(no Confl)S1⇒SCL(T)ConflictS2(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;B^{\prime};0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{$\ast$}}S_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{$\ast$(no Confl)}}S_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{Conflict}}S_{2}

where S0S_{0} is not a conflict state, and any state T0T_{0} reached from (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) in a reasonable ICLF run and weakly associated with S0S_{0}, there exists a sequence of reasonable ICLF rule applications of the rules Instantiate, InstanceDel, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom, Restart, Decide and Propagate from T0T_{0} to a state T1T_{1} that is associated with S1S_{1}, and Conflict can be applied to T1T_{1} following a reasonable strategy, reaching a state T2T_{2} that is associated with S2S_{2}.

Proof.

Since S0S_{0} is not a conflict state and Conflict was not applied to get from S0S_{0} to S1S_{1}, only Propagate, Decide and Grow can have been applied to get from S0S_{0} to S1S_{1}. In particular, the sets of initial and learned clauses in S0S_{0} and S1S_{1} are the same. Let M¯\overline{M} be the trail of S1S_{1}. We begin by applying Restart to T0T_{0} to empty the trail, which is clearly possible because T0T_{0} is weakly associated with S0S_{0}, so it is not a conflict state. Now we apply Decide with all background literals in M¯\overline{M} in any order. If this is not possible because the corresponding atom is not contained in the current set of ground atoms, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom is applied first. All added literals are propositionally undefined before their addition because we emptied the trail using Restart before and all literals in M¯\overline{M} are unique. Conflict also does not become applicable because this would imply the presence of a clause consisting only of background literals, which is equivalent to the empty clause in the context of SCL(T). Now, following the order of M¯\overline{M}, we add the foreground literals in M¯\overline{M} using Propagate and Decide, according to their annotations in M¯\overline{M}, using InstanceDel, Instantiate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom as needed, analogously to the proof of Theorem 21. For the propagations, we use the respective clause that was used in SCL(T). This is always possible because all background literals from M¯\overline{M} are on the trail. This does not violate the conditions of a reasonable run because in a regular SCL(T) run, Conflict has precedence over all other rules, Decide does not enable an application of the rule Conflict and ICLF has the same clause set as SCL(T) in this situation. The fact that we added all background literals first cannot cause any conflicts because Conflict is applicable in SCL(T) if the foreground literals are propositionally false and the background literals are 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable. Now we potentially apply InstanceDel and Instantiate to enable the application of Conflict, analogously to the proof of Theorem 21. The state T1T_{1} reached like this is associated with S1S_{1}. Since T0T_{0} is weakly associated with S0S_{0}, the sets of clauses are equal. Clearly, the sets of literals on the trail are also equal, the foreground literals are in the same order, the propagations and decisions are annotated as claimed and the background literals form a prefix of the trail. After applying Conflict with the respective clause to T1T_{1}, we reach a state T2T_{2} that is associated with S2S_{2}. ∎

Theorem 25 (Simulation of Learning).

Consider a regular SCL(T) run

(ε;N′;∅;B′;0;⊤)⇒SCL(T)∗S0⇒SCL(T)ConflictS1⇒SCL(T){Resolve,Factorize,Skip}∗S2(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;B^{\prime};0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{$\ast$}}S_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{Conflict}}S_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(T)}}^{\text{$\{\text{Resolve},\text{Factorize},\text{Skip}\}^{\ast}$}}S_{2}

and a state T1T_{1} reached from (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) in a reasonable ICLF run and associated with S1S_{1}. Then there is a state T2T_{2} reachable from T1T_{1} by applying the rules Resolve and Factorize in a reasonable way such that T2T_{2} is associated with S2S_{2}. Moreover, if Backtrack can be applied to S2S_{2} in a regular run, reaching a state S3S_{3}, then BacktrackClassic is applicable to T2T_{2} following a reasonable strategy, reaching a state T3T_{3} that is weakly associated with S3S_{3}.

Proof.

The proof of the first claim is by induction on the number of rules applied to reach S2S_{2} from S1S_{1}. For the base case, T2:=T1T_{2}:=T_{1} is obviously associated with S2S_{2}. For the induction step, let S′S^{\prime} be the state that S2S_{2} was reached from and T′T^{\prime} be reachable from T1T_{1} as claimed and associated with S′S^{\prime}. If the rule applied to S′S^{\prime} to reach S2S_{2} is Skip, T2:=T′T_{2}:=T^{\prime} is already associated with S2S_{2}. If the applied rule is Resolve, then Resolve can be applied to T′T^{\prime} to reach T2T_{2} because T′T^{\prime} is associated with S′S^{\prime}, so the propagation used by Resolve is also on the trail of T′T^{\prime}. The conflict clauses in S2S_{2} and T2T_{2} are the same because SCL(T) exhaustively factorizes the annotated clause while propagating, whereas ICLF exhaustively factorizes it while resolving, and the respective trails and clause sets do not change, so T2T_{2} is associated with S2S_{2}. If the applied rule is Factorize, then Factorize can be applied to T′T^{\prime}, reaching a state T2T_{2} that is associated with S2S_{2}.

Now assume that T2=(Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)T_{2}=(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) is associated with S2S_{2} and Backtrack is applicable to S2S_{2} in a regular SCL(T) run. Let S2=(M¯,K¯i+1,M′¯;N¯;U¯CLOSE;S_{2}=(\overline{M},\overline{K}^{i+1},\overline{M^{\prime}};\overline{N};\overline{U}; B¯;k¯;(Λ¯∥D¯∨L¯)⋅σ¯)\overline{B};\overline{k};(\overline{\Lambda}\parallel\overline{D}\lor\overline{L})\cdot\overline{\sigma}). Further, let Γ=Γ1​Γ2​K¯j​Γ3\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2}\overline{K}^{j}\Gamma_{3} such that Γ1\Gamma_{1} contains exactly all background literals of Γ\Gamma. It is possible to split Γ\Gamma like this because T2T_{2} is associated with S2S_{2}. Additionally, it holds that D⋅τ=(Λ¯∥D¯∨L¯)⋅σ¯D\cdot\tau=(\overline{\Lambda}\parallel\overline{D}\lor\overline{L})\cdot\overline{\sigma}. Since the foreground literals on the trail of S2S_{2} are a subsequence of the literals in Γ\Gamma, comp⁡(L¯​σ¯)\comp(\overline{L}\overline{\sigma}) must be contained in K¯j​Γ3\overline{K}^{j}\Gamma_{3} and the complements of the literals in D¯​σ¯\overline{D}\overline{\sigma} must be contained in Γ2\Gamma_{2}. Obviously, the literals in Λ¯​σ¯\overline{\Lambda}\overline{\sigma} must be contained in Γ1\Gamma_{1}. Hence, BacktrackClassic can be applied to T2T_{2} reaching a state T3T_{3} that is weakly associated with S3S_{3} because ICLF learns the same clause as SCL(T). Applying BacktrackClassic in this situation does not violate the reasonable strategy. For a contradiction, assume that the rightmost literal LL in Γ\Gamma occurs in D​τD\tau. The conflict clause would be the empty clause in the context of SCL(T) if LL was a background literal because the background literals form a prefix of Γ\Gamma, and since Backtrack is not applicable on the empty clause in SCL(T), LL must be a foreground literal. None of the rules applied to reach T2T_{2} from T1T_{1} changes the trail or introduces literals further to the right, so LL must have occurred in the conflict clause in T1T_{1}, hence also in S1S_{1}. Moreover, since the foreground literals on the trail of S1S_{1} form a subsequence of the foreground literals on the trail of T1T_{1} and the conflict clauses are the same, LL must occur in the conflict clause of S1S_{1} and it must be the rightmost foreground literal on the trail of S1S_{1}. However, in a regular SCL(T) run, Resolve resolves away at least the rightmost foreground literal from the trail, contradiction. ∎

Together, Theorems 24 and 25 show how ICLF can simulate a given regular SCL(T) derivation of the empty clause. Clearly, the start state of ICLF is weakly associated with the start state of SCL(T). Whenever Conflict is applied in SCL(T), ICLF can reach an associated conflict state by Theorem 24. Then, all applications of Resolve, Factorize and Skip during conflict analysis in SCL(T) can be simulated in ICLF by Theorem 25. If SCL(T) derives the empty clause during conflict analysis, ICLF also derives it because the states are shown to be associated. If SCL(T) learns a clause, then by Theorem 25, ICLF can learn the same clause, reaching a weakly associated state from which the described procedure can be iterated.

Next, we show that ICLF can simulate the Isabelle/HOL verified calculus CDCL_W [7]. CDCL is an algorithm for pure propositional logic, so we assume 𝒯\mathcal{T} to be the free theory. For easier notation, given a ground clause DD, we assume that D=D⋅{}D=D\cdot\{\}. To accommodate the different notations in ICLF and CDCL_W, we assume that Lj=L†L^{j}=L^{\dagger} for ground literals LL, and that the trail in CDCL_W grows to the right instead of to the left.

Definition 26.

We say that an ICLF state (Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) is associated with a given CDCL_W state (M¯,N¯,U¯,D¯)(\overline{M};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{D}) if clauses⁡(G)=N¯∪U¯\clauses(G)=\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}, D⋅τ=D¯D\cdot\tau=\overline{D}, when D⋅τ=⊤D\cdot\tau=\top, then Γ=M¯\Gamma=\overline{M}, and when D⋅τ≠⊤D\cdot\tau\neq\top, then M¯\overline{M} is a prefix of Γ\Gamma.

From its start state, ICLF first has to instantiate all given clauses to reach a state that is associated with the CDCL_W start state. Then, each rule application in CDCL_W can be simulated by at most one rule application in ICLF.

Theorem 27 (ICLF Simulates CDCL_W).

Let N′N^{\prime} be a propositional clause set. Then for any reasonable CDCL_W run

(ε;N′;∅;⊤)=S0⇒CDCL_WS1⇒CDCL_W…⇒CDCL_WSm,(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;\top)=S_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{CDCL\_\hskip-1.5ptW{}}}^{\text{}}S_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{CDCL\_\hskip-1.5ptW{}}}^{\text{}}\dots\Rightarrow_{\text{{CDCL\_\hskip-1.5ptW{}}}}^{\text{}}S_{m},

there exists a reasonable ICLF run

(∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)⇒ICLFInstantiate ∗T0⇒ICLF≤1T1⇒ICLF≤1…⇒ICLF≤1Tm(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{Instantiate $\ast$}}T_{0}\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 1$}}T_{1}\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 1$}}\dots\Rightarrow_{\text{ICLF{}}}^{\text{$\leq 1$}}T_{m}

such that for all i∈{0,…,m}i\in\{0,\dots,m\}, TiT_{i} is associated with SiS_{i}. After the initial applications of Instantiate, only the ICLF rules Propagate, Decide, Conflict, Restart, InstanceDel, Resolve and BacktrackClassic are needed.

Proof.

To reach T0T_{0} from the start state, Instantiate is applied with all clauses in N′N^{\prime} and the substitution {}\{\}. The reached state is clearly associated with S0S_{0}. Now the proof is by induction on mm. Assume Tm′T_{m^{\prime}} is associated with Sm′S_{m^{\prime}} and a CDCL_W rule is applied to Sm′S_{m^{\prime}} to reach Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}. By a case distinction on the applied rule, we show that we can apply at most one ICLF rule to reach a state Tm′+1T_{m^{\prime}+1} that is associated with Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}. Let Tm′=(Θ,Γ,N,G,k,D⋅τ)T_{m^{\prime}}=(\Theta;\Gamma;N;G;k;D\cdot\tau) and Sm′=(M¯,N¯,U¯,D¯)S_{m^{\prime}}=(\overline{M};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{D}). Propagate can be simulated by Propagate; the sets of ground clauses clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G) and N¯∪U¯\overline{N}\cup\overline{U} are equal and the conditions of the two rules are the same. Decide can be simulated by Decide; the ground literal must be contained in Θ\Theta because it is contained in N¯\overline{N} and hence also in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G), the remaining conditions of the two rules are the same. Conflict can be simulated by Conflict; the used clause is also contained in clauses⁡(G)\clauses(G), moreover it is unique by Corollary 13. Restart can be simulated by Restart with Γ1=ε\Gamma_{1}=\varepsilon. Forget can be simulated by InstanceDel. Again, by Corollary 13, the deleted clause occurs in GG at most once. If Skip was the applied rule, Tm′+1:=Tm′T_{m^{\prime}+1}:=T_{m^{\prime}} is already associated with Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}. Resolve can be simulated by Resolve. If the applied rule was Jump, then let M¯=M​K†​M′\overline{M}=MK^{\dagger}M^{\prime} and D¯=D′∨L\overline{D}=D^{\prime}\lor L such that LL has the level of the state Sm′S_{m^{\prime}}. It follows that D′D^{\prime} is propositionally false in MM and LL is propositionally undefined in MM, so BacktrackClassic is applicable to Tm′T_{m^{\prime}}, restoring the equality of the trails and hence reaching a state Tm′+1T_{m^{\prime}+1} that is associated with Sm′+1S_{m^{\prime}+1}. BacktrackClassic is indeed applicable following a reasonable strategy because in CDCL, due to exhaustive propagation, Resolve must be applied at least once before Jump becomes applicable. ∎

In standard presentations of CDCL(T) [30, 4], conflict analysis is left flexible, allowing different learning mechanisms. We therefore do not state a formal simulation theorem for CDCL(T). Since ICLF learns only non-redundant clauses, such a theorem would have to impose a compatible condition on learning in CDCL(T). We can nevertheless describe how ICLF, given a theory solver for 𝒯\mathcal{T}, can be used to decide the satisfiability of a ground clause set modulo 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Remark 28 (ICLF Simulates CDCL(T)).

Let N′N^{\prime} be a set of ground clauses modulo a theory 𝒯\mathcal{T}. We start in the state (∅;ε;N′;∅;0;⊤)(\emptyset;\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;0;\top) and first apply Instantiate with {}\{\} to all clauses in N′N^{\prime}. Now, by Theorems 14 and 15, applying the rules Decide, Propagate, Conflict, Restart, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict, Explain, Resolve and BacktrackClassic according to a reasonable strategy and restricting Restart, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom to a finite number of applications, ICLF either derives the empty clause, or it terminates in a state whose trail is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-satisfiable model of N′N^{\prime}.

For instantiation-based SMT procedures combining quantifier instantiation with CDCL(T), we are not aware of any formal description. Nevertheless, ICLF can model the essential interaction between an instantiation module and a CDCL(T) solver. The process consists of two phases: the instantiation phase and the CDCL(T) phase. First, the instantiation module generates some instances, including all of the initially ground clauses, using Instantiate. Then, CDCL(T) is run according to Remark 28. If it derives unsatisfiability, the process terminates. Otherwise, the instantiation module adds more instances. In ICLF, due to non-ground learning, the instantiation module can also instantiate learned clauses, which is not possible in classical instantiation-based SMT solving.

There are other calculi that integrate explicit model building and a form of clause learning. Theory instantiation [18] extends the InstGen [17] calculus with theories. Still, only instances of existing clauses are learned with respect to ground theory conflicts. The model-building in model evolution with lemma learning [5] goes beyond ground literals but does not involve theories. Lemma learning gets more complicated and no non-redundancy guarantees are presented. In conflict resolution [38] models are built by first-order decision literals and propagations computed by the unit propagation rule. The conflict resolution rule and the overall calculus are described in an abstract way, such that no quality guarantees are possible with respect to newly generated clauses.

5 Conclusion

We presented the calculus ICLF for non-ground SMT, which generalizes several model-based approaches for propositional logic, first-order logic, and first-order logic modulo theories. Most notably, ICLF extends quantifier instantiation with non-ground learning and a tighter integration of instantiation and model building. It also extends SCL by allowing a lazier treatment of non-ground clauses: conflicts only have to be considered for the current ground instances. In this way, ICLF provides a flexible setting for combining techniques from instantiation-based SMT solving and non-ground clause learning. The long-term goal is to use this flexibility to develop new methods for solving problems that are beyond the reach of current solvers.

The main direction for future work is to implement ICLF and integrate its ideas into existing solvers. Since ICLF generalizes multiple other calculi, it naturally leaves freedom in several choices. One such choice is which ground instances to create and when to create them. This difficulty already arises in quantifier instantiation and in SCL, and we hope that instantiation techniques that have proved useful in SMT solving [15, 14, 20, 37, 36] can also be adapted to ICLF. Another such choice is when, and to what extent, to check the applicability of theory rules, for instance when to perform complete checks. This depends on the specific theory, and we expect that strategies that work well in CDCL(T) will also work well in ICLF. As in all model-based calculi, there is also freedom in the choice of which literals to include in the model, that is, which decisions and propagations to perform. Unlike in SCL, however, decisions and propagations are restricted by the current ground instances in ICLF. Finally, there is freedom in the choice of how to explain theory propagations and conflicts. In CDCL(T), it is sufficient to explain a theory conflict by a minimal subset of contradictory trail literals, for example the literals h⁡(a)=g⁡(a)h(a)=g(a), h⁡(a)=ah(a)=a, and g⁡(a)≠ag(a)\neq a from Example 4. In ICLF, this ground explanation can be used, but it may be preferable to use the more general explanation x2≠x3∨x2≠x4∨x3=x4x_{2}\neq x_{3}\lor x_{2}\neq x_{4}\lor x_{3}=x_{4}, a theory lemma expressing the transitivity axiom for equality. Instantiated with the substitution {x2↦h(a),x3↦g(a),x4↦a}\{x_{2}\mapsto h(a),x_{3}\mapsto g(a),x_{4}\mapsto a\}, this yields the same ground explanation, but at the non-ground level it allows us to learn a more general clause from the conflict. If we use the ground explanation directly, by contrast, then all variables matched against the ground explanation are grounded, and this restricts our ability to learn non-ground clauses. Thus, besides instantiation heuristics, a central challenge for implementing ICLF is to develop theory solvers that can produce useful non-ground explanations [3, 25].

This gives another perspective on the role of theory explanations in ICLF. In saturation-based theorem proving, adding theory axioms as ordinary clauses can greatly enlarge the search space [34, 21, 23]. In ICLF, theory axioms need not be added to NN as clauses available for arbitrary instantiation, propagation, and resolution. Instead, theory lemmas only have to be produced when they become relevant during conflict analysis. In this way, the ground search guides the use of theory lemmas in resolution, rather than making all theory axioms available throughout the search. This allows theory reasoning to contribute non-ground theory lemmas when the ground search needs them, combining the control of model-guided reasoning with the generality of first-order learning.

Appendix A Further Examples

Example 29.

This example shows that the 1UIP clause can be redundant in chronological backtracking. Consider the propositional clause set N={P,¬P∨¬R∨S,¬V∨U,¬V∨¬U,T∨V∨U,T∨V∨¬U,¬P∨¬T∨V,¬R∨¬S∨¬T∨V}N=\{P,\neg P\lor\neg R\lor S,\neg V\lor U,\neg V\lor\neg U,T\lor V\lor U,T\lor V\lor\neg U,\neg P\lor\neg T\lor V,\neg R\lor\neg S\lor\neg T\lor V\}. We use the calculus by Möhle and Biere [27], but omit δ\delta and annotate the levels on the trail instead. This means that our states are two-tuples (N;M)(N;M) where NN is the clause set and MM is the trail. We always use the 1UIP clause for backtracking and always perform chronological backtracking, i.e., we always jump to the previous decision level.

Appendix B Further Lemmas

Lemma 30 (Stuck SCL(FOL) States Are Stuck in ICLF).

If

(ε;N′;∅;β′;0;⊤)⇒SCL(FOL)∗(Γ¯;N¯;U¯;β¯;k¯;D¯⋅τ¯)=:S(\varepsilon;N^{\prime};\emptyset;\beta^{\prime};0;\top)\Rightarrow_{\text{SCL(FOL)}}^{\text{$\ast$}}(\overline{\Gamma};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{\beta};\overline{k};\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau})=:S

in a regular SCL(FOL) run, no rule except Grow is applicable to SS,

in a reasonable ICLF run and TT is associated with SS, then no ICLF rule except Instantiate, ClauseDel, InstanceDel, AtomDel, Restart, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Learn and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom is applicable to TT.

Moreover, there is no atom A≺Bβ¯A\prec_{B}\overline{\beta} such that AA is a ground instance of an atom in atom⁡(N)\atom(N) and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom is applicable with AA.

Proof.

The rule Explain is not applicable in the free theory because no undefined literals can be theory-propagated from a consistent trail in the free theory. If no rules except Grow are applicable to (Γ¯,N¯,U¯,β¯,k¯,D¯⋅τ¯)(\overline{\Gamma};\overline{N};\overline{U};\overline{\beta};\overline{k};\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}), then either D¯⋅τ¯=⊥\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\bot and N¯\overline{N} is unsatisfiable, or D¯⋅τ¯=⊤\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\top, gnd(N)≺Bβ¯\gnd(N)^{\prec_{B}\overline{\beta}} is satisfiable and Γ¯⊧gnd(N)≺Bβ¯\overline{\Gamma}\models\gnd(N)^{\prec_{B}\overline{\beta}} [13, Theorem 10].

If D¯⋅τ¯=⊥\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\bot, then D⋅τ=⊥D\cdot\tau=\bot as well because TT is associated with SS. Clearly, no rule except Explain can be applied to TT in this case, and as argued earlier, Explain is not applicable in the free theory.

Otherwise, D⋅τ=D¯⋅τ¯=⊤D\cdot\tau=\overline{D}\cdot\overline{\tau}=\top and Γ¯⊧gnd(N)≺Bβ¯\overline{\Gamma}\models\gnd(N)^{\prec_{B}\overline{\beta}}. We claim that there is no atom A∈ΘA\in\Theta such that AA is propositionally undefined on the trail. If there was such an atom AA, then A≺Bβ¯A\prec_{B}\overline{\beta} and there would be a clause C∈N=N¯∪U¯C\in N=\overline{N}\cup\overline{U} such that AA is a ground instance of a literal in CC. It follows that Decide would be applicable to SS, contradiction. For each rule that we claim that it is not applicable to TT, we argue why. For Resolve, Factorize, BacktrackClassic, BacktrackFOL and BacktrackCB, it is obvious that they are not applicable to TT because D⋅τ=⊤D\cdot\tau=\top. For Decide, Propagate and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Propagate, this follows from the fact that there is no propositionally undefined atom in Θ\Theta. If Conflict was applicable to TT, that is, if there was a C⋅σ∈GC\cdot\sigma\in G such that C​σC\sigma is propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, then by Item 1 of Lemma 5, C∈N¯∪U¯C\in\overline{N}\cup\overline{U}, so Conflict would be applicable to SS, contradiction. If 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Atom was applicable with an atom A≺Bβ¯A\prec_{B}\overline{\beta} that is a ground instance of an atom in atom⁡(N)\atom(N), then Decide would be applicable to SS because AA is undefined in Γ\Gamma and Γ¯\overline{\Gamma} by Item 2 of Lemma 5, contradiction. Since 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the free theory and Γ\Gamma is consistent, no theory-valid clause can be propositionally false in Γ\Gamma, so 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict is not applicable to TT. ∎

Appendix C A Strategy to Apply BacktrackCB

In the conclusion of their paper, Möhle and Biere [27] suspect that chronological backtracking can also be applied in SMT. Following this, we incorporate a rule BacktrackCB that allows to backtrack in a way that is similar to chronological backtracking. However, in the context of SMT, a few challenges arise that do not occur in pure SAT solving. Most importantly, with theory propagations, the actual decision level, called asserting level by Möhle and Biere, of propagated literals is not always known. This affects not only the theory propagated literals, but also the literals propagated from these literals. As explaining theory propagations can be expensive, we aim for a conflict analysis procedure that needs to explain as little as possible. This results in three key changes in comparison to the procedure described by Möhle and Biere. First, we do not define our procedure based on decision levels, but based on reachable literals from the rightmost implying decision L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} instead. This means that no literals to the left of this decision L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} need to be explained. Second, instead of keeping all literals implied by decisions to the left of L′j+1L^{\prime j+1}, we only keep, in addition to all literals to the left of L′j+1L^{\prime j+1}, those literals to the right of L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} that are in reach−1\reach^{-1} of the learned clause, but not implied by L′L^{\prime}. This is because these literals are necessary to propagate from the learned clause, and for any other literal to the right of L′j+1L^{\prime j+1}, we would first have to find its actual decision level, possibly causing unnecessary explaining. Third, whereas their procedure allows backtracking to any decision level between the one at which the learned clause propagates and jj, we only allow backtracking to decision level jj, resulting in a much simpler definition. Otherwise, all theory propagations between L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} and the point to which we backtrack would have to be explained.

In the following, we describe how the rules Explain, Resolve and BacktrackCB can be used to perform conflict analysis on a ground conflict clause D′D^{\prime} with chronological backtracking. Let D′=D′′∨L′′D^{\prime}=D^{\prime\prime}\lor L^{\prime\prime} such that comp⁡(L′′)\comp(L^{\prime\prime}) occurs rightmost on the trail among the complements of literals in D′D^{\prime}. If comp⁡(L′′)\comp(L^{\prime\prime}) is a decision, then by Lemma 8, the conflict was reached by 𝒯\mathcal{T}-Conflict and BacktrackCB can be applied immediately. Otherwise, Resolve should be applied to comp⁡(L′′)\comp(L^{\prime\prime}), which possibly requires explaining it first. This ensures learning a non-redundant clause, and is required in a reasonable strategy [Definition 2]. We call the resulting clause DD. Then, using Appendix C on DD, we identify the rightmost implying decision L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} and mark all literals in reach⁡(L′)∩⋃L∈Dreach−1⁡(comp⁡(L))\reach(L^{\prime})\cap\bigcup_{L\in D}\reach^{-1}(\comp(L)). Now, we can work backwards along the trail until we reach L′j+1L^{\prime j+1} to compute the learned clause. When we encounter a literal whose complement occurs in the current conflict clause, then if it is not marked, we push it to a stack. We also push all predecessors of literals on the stack to the stack, which can be managed by a second mark. If the literal is the only marked trail literal whose complement occurs in the current conflict clause, then we skip it, as its complement is the literal that will be propagated from the learned clause. If the literal is one of several marked trail literals whose complements occur in the current conflict clause, then we apply Resolve on it exhaustively, or we apply Factorize exhaustively and then Resolve. Note that it is not necessary anymore to use Explain because all literals that are resolved now have been explained in Appendix C. In all other cases, i.e., if the complement of the literal does not occur in the current conflict clause and is also not the predecessor of any literal on the stack, we can safely skip this literal. In the state that is reached by this procedure, BacktrackCB is applicable.

 

Algorithm 1 Preparation for conflict analysis with BacktrackCB

 
1: function PrepareConflictAnalysisCB(conflict clause DD)
2:   children←\textit{children}\leftarrow data structure to store for each literal a list of literals
3:   pq←\textit{pq}\leftarrow priority queue ordered by trail position (largest first)
4:   for L∈DL\in D do
5:    pq.insert​(comp⁡(L))\textit{pq}.\text{insert}(\comp(L))   
6:   while !pq.empty()!\textit{pq}.\text{empty}() and pq.front​()\textit{pq}.\text{front}() is not a decision do
7:    L←pq.pop​()L\leftarrow\textit{pq}.\text{pop}()
8:    if LL is a theory propagation then
9:      explain​(L)\text{explain}(L)    
10:    for K∈parents​(L)K\in\text{parents}(L) do
11:      children​[K].insert​(L)\textit{children}[K].\text{insert}(L)
12:      if KK not in pq then
13:       pq.insert​(K)\textit{pq}.\text{insert}(K)           
14:   if pq.empty​()\textit{pq}.\text{empty}() then
15:    return UNSAT   
16:   DFS from pq.front​()\textit{pq}.\text{front}() using children, mark all visited literals
